Κάποιος κάποτε είπε «Όταν η ελπίδα είναι ζωντανή, η νύχτα είναι λιγότερο σκοτεινή, η μοναξιά λιγότερο βαθιά και ο φόβος λιγότερο έντονος.» Όταν δούλευα σε φυλακή ως βοηθός ιεροκήρυκα, καθόμουν με τους καταδικασμένους άνδρες και άκουγα να μιλούν για τη δυσκολία τους. Σχεδόν χωρίς εξαίρεση, όλοι έλεγαν ότι ελπίζουν κάποια μέρα να βγουν από τη φυλακή. Ακόμη και αν είχαν ισόβια, ελπίζαν ότι θα βγουν.

Έχω μιλήσει με ανθρώπους που δεν ομολογούν ότι είναι γεννημένοι ξανά, αλλά παρ’ όλα αυτά ελπίζουν να πάνε στον ουρανό. Αυτοί οι άνθρωποι δεν τολμούν να σταματήσουν να ελπίζουν. Η ελπίδα τους βασίζεται στην ίδια τους την ελπίδα! Μια δίαιτα πάνω σε αυτό το είδος ελπίδας είναι σίγουρα φτωχή! Αυτή η σκέψη μου θυμίζει τα λόγια του Ιησού στον Ιωάννη 10:1-2 για την είσοδο στο μαντρί: «Αλλά όποιος μπαίνει από την πύλη είναι ο ποιμένας των προβάτων.» Οι άνθρωποι χτίζουν την ελπίδα τους για τον ουρανό σε πολλά ασταθή θεμέλια. Κάποιοι βασίζουν την ελπίδα τους στο ότι βαπτίστηκαν σε μια ορισμένη εκκλησία. Κάποιοι ελπίζουν στη συμμετοχή τους στην εκκλησία. Κάποιοι ελπίζουν στα καλά τους έργα, ενώ άλλοι ελπίζουν στην ελπίδα τους. Η Αγία Γραφή, όμως, λέει, «...εκτός αν κάποιος γεννηθεί άνωθεν, δεν μπορεί να ιδεί τη βασιλεία του Θεού» (Ιωάννης 3:3).

Υπάρχει αληθινή ελπίδα και ψευδής ελπίδα. Η ψευδής ελπίδα είναι το «να ανεβαίνει κάποιος από άλλο δρόμο», ενώ η αληθινή ελπίδα είναι «ο όποιος μπαίνει από την πύλη.»

«Διότι σωθήκαμε με την ελπίδα· αλλά η ελπίδα που έχει γίνει πραγματικότητα δεν είναι πια ελπίδα· διότι, αν κάποιος βλέπει, γιατί να ελπίζει ακόμα;» (Ρωμαίους 8:24). Αυτή η λέξη ελπίδα σημαίνει «με προσμονή ή μεγάλη προσδοκία.» Μπορούμε να πούμε ότι είμαστε σωσμένοι με μεγάλη προσδοκία; Ναι, μπορούμε. «Μην κοπιάζετε για το ψωμί που φθείρεται, αλλά για το ψωμί που μένει προς ζωήν αιώνιον, που θα σας το δώσει ο Υιός του ανθρώπου· διότι αυτόν έχει σφραγίσει ο Θεός, ο Πατέρας» (Ιωάννης 6:27). Αυτό φαίνεται σαν κάποιο είδος αντίφασης. Δεν σώζομεθα άραγε από τη χάρη; Ναι, σώζομεθα από τη χάρη δια της πίστεως (Εφεσίους 2:8). Τότε τι σημαίνει αυτό το «σωζόμαστε δια της ελπίδος» και το να εργαζόμαστε για «το ψωμί το μένον εις ζωὴν αιώνιον»;

«Τότε του είπαν, τι λοιπόν δει να ποιήσωμεν, ίνα τα έργα του Θεού ποιώμεν;» Ο Ιησούς απάντησε και τους είπε, «Τούτο εστί το έργον του Θεού, ίνα πιστεύητε εις τον ον απέστειλεν αυτόν» (Ιωάννης 6:28-29). Μόνον διά της χάριτος σώζομεθα, αλλά όπως υποδηλώνει αυτή η περικοπή, η χάρις θέτει έναν όρο. Ο όρος της χάριτος είναι να πιστεύσουμε σε Αυτόν. Ένας άλλος όρος της σωτηρίας είναι η μετάνοια (Μάρκος 1:15), ενώ άλλος είναι το ανέβασμα του σταυρού. «Όποιος θέλει να έρθει πίσω μου, να αρνηθεί τον εαυτό του, να σηκώσει τον σταυρό του και να με ακολουθήσει» (Μάρκος 8:34).

Όλα όσα θα κάναμε για τον Χριστό, είτε είναι πίστη, μετάνοια ή ανέβασμα του σταυρού, είναι από χάρη. Οτιδήποτε έχουμε ή κάνουμε είναι εξαιτίας Του. Δεν εργαζόμαστε για τη σωτηρία μας, διότι ο Χριστός ο ίδιος είπε, «Τετέλεσται.» Δεν έχουμε τίποτα για να ελπίζουμε αν δεν εκπληρώνουμε τους όρους της σωτηρίας μας. Μόλις δεχθούμε τον Κύριο Ιησού ως Σωτήρα, τότε «η ελπίς δεν καταισχύνει» (Ρωμαίους 5:5).

Καθώς ο Χριστός ζωντανεύει μέσα μας, Τον αγαπάμε και επιλέγουμε να Τον υπακούσουμε. Ο Ιησούς γίνεται πιο πολύτιμος σε εμάς καθώς ωριμάζουμε στη χριστιανική μας ζωή. Καθώς η σχέση μας μεγαλώνει, μεγαλώνει και η προσδοκία μας. Όσο περισσότερο Τον γνωρίζουμε, τόσο περισσότερο ανυπομονούμε να βρεθούμε στην παρουσία Του. Καθώς αυξάνεται η προσμονή μας να Τον δούμε, προσπαθούμε να κάνουμε ό,τι είναι δυνατό για να τον ευχαριστήσουμε. Ο έντονος ζήλος μας μας προστατεύει από το να κουραστούμε, έτσι «σωζόμαστε διά της ελπίδος.»

Είναι η ελπίδα σου σαν αυτήν που «ανεβαίνει από άλλο δρόμο», ή σαν αυτήν «που μπαίνει από την πύλη»; Έχεις μια βάση για την ελπίδα σου ή είναι μια άδεια ελπίδα που δεν έχει θεμέλιο;

Ελπίζω να ωριμάζεις «...εις αυτόν εν παντί, ος είναι η κεφαλή, ο Χριστός» (Εφεσίους 4:15).

Ελπίζω να μεγαλώσεις κι άλλο, ώστε και η προσδοκία σου να δεις τον Χριστό να αυξηθεί. Η μαρτυρία αυτής της προσδοκίας είναι, «...για αυτό στενάζουμε και ποθούμε σφοδρά να ντυθούμε με την κατοικία μας που είναι από τον ουρανό» (Β΄ Κορινθίους 5:2).

Greetings in the worthy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. As I gaze out across the barren January landscape, I can’t help but wonder what this new year will bring. Undoubtedly, it will bring a mixture of joy and sorrow, excitement and drear, laughter and tears, and everything else in between, which only an Almighty Creator God can arrange in such a way that will magnify His worthy power and excellence. Yet our finite, negative minds tend to anticipate all the bad things that could happen. Will inflation drive food prices even higher? Will widespread fighting erupt across the Middle East? What will happen in the elections? Will the losing party resort to protests and rioting?

I suppose, since the fall of man, these fear-driven thoughts have roamed through the minds of humanity at the beginning of each year. Yet, as it is so aptly pointed out by the writer of the article, “God’s Faithfulness Manifest Even in the Curse”, God has kindly provided for humanity since the beginning of time. Looking back at God’s faithfulness to man over the centuries, we have no reason to doubt God will do the same for us in 2024.

Despite God’s faithfulness to us, the effects of the fall of man are still evident. Family members get sick, church and relationship struggles rob us of sleep, the checkbook runs dry, the children squabble and cry, and the demands of our schedules have us hopping from one event to the next. And sometimes, it seems that all these calamities hit us at the same time. Our bodies and minds are not created to handle this. We become weary. Bone tired. Exhausted to the point when even thinking hurts. We face burnout. In this issue, “A Word From the Doctor” guides us as we face the maze of life, giving us practical and Biblical solutions to avoid or recover from burnout. He writes, “Jesus knows our limitations. He wants us to have balance, living in such a way that we not only have strength for today but also for tomorrow, next week, and next year – till He comes again.”

Perhaps one good remedy to reduce the stress of life would be to go for a bike ride. But we need to be careful and avoid getting into a bike race like the two lads did in this issue’s children’s story. We may end up with more stress than we bargained for.

Despite our best efforts to live stress-free lives, we still meet with the unexpected. Last week I was cleaning out our broiler houses in preparation for a new flock. I leaned across the tractor fender to push a partly opened door out of the way. As I stood up, my foot accidentally hit the hydrostatic pedal, lurching the tractor forward and throwing me off-balance. My foot somehow got caught under the pedal, and for a split second, I feared I would fall right in front of the rear wheel. In a last-ditch effort, I threw myself away from the tractor. My foot slipped out of my shoe, and I landed unharmed on the ground. The tractor slowly headed off with my shoe still wedged under the pedal. All ended well, and a few lessons were learned. It was nothing other than the providence of God that prevented a freak incident from becoming a bad accident. Truly I agree with Solomon, “For the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken” (Proverbs 3:26).

As we navigate through this year, let’s join the hymnwriter in worship, where he writes:

When all Thy mercies, O my God,
My rising soul surveys,
Transported with the view, I’m lost
In wonder, love and praise.

It is only by the mercies of an all-loving God that we have life and breath. May we give our all to Him and to the work of His kingdom in heartfelt thanksgiving for His unspeakable gift.

Blessings to all,

Edward Martin

거룩하신 주 예수 그리스도의 이름으로 문안드립니다. 황량한 1월 풍경을 바라보며 새해가 무엇을 가져올지 생각하지 않을 수 없습니다. 틀림없이 기쁨과 슬픔, 흥분과 권태, 웃음과 눈물, 그리고 전능하신 창조주 하나님만이 그분의 거룩하신 능력과 탁월함을 영화롭게 하도록 배치하실 수 있는 온갖 것들이 뒤섞여 올 것입니다. 그러나 유한하고 부정적인 우리의 마음은 일어날 수 있는 모든 나쁜 일들을 먼저 예상하는 경향이 있습니다. 물가 상승이 식료품 가격을 더 끌어올릴 것인가? 중동 전역에서 광범위한 전투가 발생할 것인가? 선거에서는 무슨 일이 일어날 것인가? 패배한 정당이 시위와 폭동에 나설 것인가?

사람의 타락 이래로 이러한 두려움에 이끌린 생각들이 해마다 새해 초마다 인류의 마음을 떠돌아다녔을 것이라고 생각합니다. 그러나 “하나님의 신실하심이 저주 속에서도 드러남”이라는 글의 필자가 적절히 지적한 바대로, 하나님은 처음부터 친절하게 인류를 돌보아 오셨습니다. 수세기 동안 하나님이 인간에게 베푸신 신실하심을 돌아볼 때, 2024년에도 하나님께서 우리에게 같은 일을 행하실 것이라고 의심할 이유가 없습니다.

하나님께서 우리에게 신실하셨음에도 불구하고, 사람의 타락의 영향은 여전히 분명합니다. 가족이 병들고, 교회와 인간관계의 문제로 잠을 설치며, 가계부의 잔액이 바닥나고, 아이들이 다투며 울고, 빽빽한 일정 때문에 우리는 이리저리 뛰어다닙니다. 때로는 이 모든 재난이 동시에 몰려오는 것처럼 보입니다. 우리의 몸과 마음은 이것을 감당하도록 창조되지 않았습니다. 우리는 지칩니다. 뼈가 지쳐 버릴 정도로. 생각하는 것조차 고통스러울 정도로 기진맥진해집니다. 우리는 번아웃을 겪습니다. 이번 호의 "의사의 한 말씀"은 삶의 미로를 헤쳐 나갈 때 우리가 번아웃을 피하거나 회복할 수 있도록 실용적이고 성경적인 해결책을 안내합니다. 그는 이렇게 씁니다. “예수님은 우리의 한계를 아십니다. 그분은 우리가 오늘뿐 아니라 내일, 다음 주, 내년까지 — 그분이 다시 오실 때까지 — 쓸 수 있는 힘을 갖고 균형 있게 살기를 바라십니다.”

삶의 스트레스를 줄이는 한 가지 좋은 처방은 자전거 타기가 될 수 있습니다. 하지만 이번 호의 아동 이야기 속 두 소년이 했던 것처럼 자전거 경주에 뛰어들지 않도록 주의해야 합니다. 우리는 예상보다 더 많은 스트레스를 안게 될 수 있습니다.

스트레스 없는 삶을 살기 위해 최선을 다해도, 우리는 여전히 예기치 못한 일을 만납니다. 지난주에 새 무리를 들일 준비로 육계장을 청소하고 있었습니다. 부분적으로 열린 문을 밀어 치우기 위해 트랙터 펜더 너머로 몸을 숙였습니다. 일어서자마자 발이 우연히 유압 페달에 닿아 트랙터가 앞으로 홱 튀어나가 균형을 잃게 했습니다. 어쩐 일인지 발이 페달 아래에 걸렸고, 순간적으로 뒷바퀴 바로 앞에 쓰러질까 두려웠습니다. 마지막 몸부림으로 저는 트랙터에서 몸을 멀리 던졌습니다. 제 발은 신발에서 벗겨졌고, 저는 다치지 않고 땅에 떨어졌습니다. 트랙터는 천천히 제 신발이 아직 페달 아래에 끼인 채로 가버렸습니다. 모든 것은 잘 끝났고, 몇 가지 교훈을 얻었습니다. 기묘한 사고가 큰 재난이 되지 않게 막아 주신 것은 다름 아닌 하나님의 섭리였습니다. 저는 솔로몬의 말씀에 전적으로 동의합니다. “여호와는 네 신뢰가 되시며 네 발이 붙잡히지 않게 지키시리라” (잠언 3:26).

이 한 해를 지나는 동안 우리는 찬송가 작가와 함께 예배로 나아갑시다. 그는 이렇게 썼습니다:

주여 모든 자비를 내가 돌아볼 때에,

"O give thanks unto the God of heaven: for His mercy endureth for ever"
—Psalm 136:26

In your journey of life, from infancy to where you are today, have you ever taken a few minutes to meditate on the mercy God has shown you? Infancy to childhood, childhood to youth, youth to adulthood, and beyond, God's everlasting mercy is upon them that fear Him! The scripture says in Deuteronomy 7:9 that the mercy of God extends way past our short lives here on earth, even to a thousand generations. Take a moment and wonder in the glory and beauty of this unchanging, eternal attribute of God!

As we take a look at the history behind this hymn, let us endeavor to see the hand of God at work in the life of the hymn writer. The hymn, "When All Thy Mercies O My God," written in 1712, has been published in 994 hymnals and is to this day in the list of the best 100 hymns ever written. As the writer nears the end of his time on earth, he reflects in this hymn his awe at the mercies of God toward him throughout his life.

Joseph Addison, born May 1, 1672, was an English essayist, poet, and man of letters. Concerning his birth, we find that he “appeared weak and unlikely to live", Mr. Tyers says.* And that “he was laid out for dead as soon as he was born.” Without doubt, the providence of God preserved his young life and gave him nearly half a century to serve Him on the earth. He was the eldest son of Lancelot Addison, a well-learned man and minister in his church. His father, being a studious man himself, made sure his son Joseph had a good education. He commenced his studies in his hometown of Milston, in Wiltshire, England.

While in school around 1685, the 13-year-old hymn writer met and became best of friends with Richard Steele, the two of them being only a few months apart in age. They continued their friendship throughout the years, and 27 years later from 1711 to 1712, they cofounded The Spectator magazine, in which this hymn was first published.

After passing through several schools, Addison went to Oxford when he was about 15 years old. While he was there, he continued to gain in learning and skill, especially in the areas of writing Latin poems and essays. By the time he was 22, in 1694, he also began to show his skill at writing English poetry.

One of the most notable details of his life that conveyed to him the mercy of God is how he managed to narrowly escape an awful shipwreck. It was this tragedy and his frightening tale of survival that would go on to inspire the writing of this uplifting hymn.

Here is the hymn with the original 13 verses:

When all Thy mercies, O my God,
My rising soul surveys,
Transported with the view,
I’m lost In wonder, love and praise.

Thy Providence my life sustained,
And all my wants redressed,
While in the silent womb I lay,
And hung upon the breast.

To all my weak complaints and cries
Thy mercy lent an ear,
Ere yet my feeble thoughts had learned,
To form themselves in prayer.

Unnumbered comforts to my soul
Thy tender care bestowed,
Before my infant heart conceived
From Whom those comforts flowed.

When in the slippery paths of youth
With heedless steps I ran,
Thine arm unseen conveyed me safe,
And led me up to man.

Through hidden dangers, toils, and deaths,
It gently cleared my way;
And through the pleasing snares of vice,
More to be feared than they.

O how shall words with equal warmth
The gratitude declare,
That glows within my ravished heart?
But thou canst read it there.

Thy bounteous hand with worldly bliss
Hath made my cup run o’er;
And, in a kind and faithful Friend,
Hath doubled all my store.

Ten thousand thousand precious gifts
My daily thanks employ;
Nor is the last a cheerful heart
That tastes those gifts with joy.

When worn with sickness, oft hast Thou
With health renewed my face;
And, when in sins and sorrows sunk,
Revived my soul with grace.

Through every period of my life
Thy goodness I’ll pursue
And after death, in distant worlds,
The glorious theme renew.

When nature fails, and day and night
Divide Thy works no more,
My ever grateful heart,
O Lord,Thy mercy shall adore.

Through all eternity to Thee
A joyful song I’ll raise;
For, oh, eternity’s too short
To utter all Thy praise!

As we endeavor to understand the life and story of the hymnologist, let's take a short look at some disappointments he faced. Being single into his 40s, he had hopes of someday having a happy marriage. His marriage to Charlotte, a widow of 15 years, didn’t turn out as he had anticipated. It is said that their courtship was long and anxious. They were married in August 1716 in his 44th year. A quote states that “He is said to have first known her by becoming tutor to her son. The marriage, if uncontradicted report can be credited, made no addition to his happiness; it neither found them nor made them equal."* In addition to his less-than-ideal marriage, the loss of his good friend Richard Steele sometime after that took a toll on him.

By the year 1717, his health began to decline rapidly, and by March 1718, he had to resign some of his work positions, having a great need for rest and quietness. "The disease under which Addison laboured appears to have been asthma. It became more violent after his retirement from office and was now accompanied by dropsy. His deathbed was placid and resigned, and comforted by those religious hopes which he had so often suggested to others..." *

One last note I will include here on the life of the hymn writer is the account of his passing. There was a young man by the name of Lord Warwick, rough and loose in character, who Addison had often tried to win to the faith, all to no avail. Nearing the end of his life, he endeavored one last attempt to impress this young man with the importance of Christianity. He sent for him to come and be present as he passed away, saying, "I have sent for you that you may see how a Christian can die." We have no record of how this experience affected Warwick’s behavior, but we can assume that it most likely did. Joseph Addison died at Holland House on the 17th of June, 1719, six weeks after his 47th birthday. He is buried in the Poet's Corner of Westminster Abbey.

This hymn has several tunes: “St Peter,” composed by Alexander Robert Reinagle in 1836, is used in the Church Hymnal and Christian Hymnary. The tune "Geneva" was composed by John Cole in 1805. He was born in Tewksbury, England, and came to the United States in his boyhood. Baltimore, Maryland became his American home, and he was educated there. Early in life, he became a musician and music publisher. He continued to compose music until his death. This tune is found in the Zion's Praises, Hymns of the Church, and Harmonia Sacra. The tune "Contemplation", composed by F.A.Gore Ouseley, is more widely used by evangelical and other church groups. Other hymns by Joseph Addison include "The Lord my Pasture Shall Prepare" and "The Spacious Firmament." Here is one final quote to help us understand who Joseph Addison was and what he believed. "His religion has nothing in it enthusiastic or superstitious; he appears neither weakly credulous nor wantonly skeptical; his morality is neither dangerously lax nor impracticably rigid. All the enchantment of fancy and all the cogency of argument are employed to recommend to the reader his real interest, the care of pleasing the Author of his being."

*sourced from Wikipedia and hymnary.org

“Rendete grazie al Dio dei cieli: poiché la sua misericordia dura in eterno”
—Salmo 136:26

Nel tuo cammino di vita, dall'infanzia fino a dove sei oggi, ti sei mai fermato qualche minuto a meditare sulla misericordia che Dio ti ha mostrato? Dall'infanzia alla fanciullezza, dalla fanciullezza all'adolescenza, dall'adolescenza all'età adulta e oltre, la misericordia eterna di Dio è su coloro che Lo temono! La Scrittura dice in Deuteronomio 7:9 che la misericordia di Dio si estende ben oltre le nostre vite brevi qui sulla terra, fino a mille generazioni. Prenditi un momento e meravigliati della gloria e della bellezza di questo attributo immutabile ed eterno di Dio!

Esaminando la storia dietro questo inno, cerchiamo di vedere la mano di Dio all'opera nella vita dell'autore del canto. L'inno, “When All Thy Mercies O My God” (Quando tutte le tue misericordie, o mio Dio), scritto nel 1712, è stato pubblicato in 994 inni e ancora oggi figura nella lista dei 100 migliori inni mai scritti. Mentre l'autore si avvicina alla fine del suo tempo sulla terra, in questo inno riflette il suo stupore per le misericordie di Dio verso di lui lungo tutta la sua vita.

Joseph Addison, nato il 1º maggio 1672, fu saggista, poeta e uomo di lettere inglese. Riguardo alla sua nascita, troviamo che “apparve debole e improbabile che vivesse", dice il sig. Tyers.* E che “fu steso come morto appena nato.” Senza dubbio la provvidenza di Dio preservò la sua vita infantile e gli diede quasi mezzo secolo per servirLo sulla terra. Era il figlio maggiore di Lancelot Addison, uomo ben istruito e ministro nella sua chiesa. Suo padre, essendo anch'egli studioso, si assicurò che suo figlio Joseph ricevessse una buona istruzione. Iniziò gli studi nella sua città natale di Milston, nel Wiltshire, Inghilterra.

Mentre era a scuola, intorno al 1685, il giovane autore dell'inno di 13 anni incontrò e divenne il migliore amico di Richard Steele, i due essendo separati da pochi mesi di età. Continuarono la loro amicizia nel corso degli anni e, 27 anni dopo, dal 1711 al 1712, cofondarono la rivista The Spectator, nella quale questo inno fu pubblicato per la prima volta.

Dopo aver frequentato varie scuole, Addison andò a Oxford quando aveva circa 15 anni. Mentre era lì continuò ad accrescere cultura e abilità, soprattutto nella scrittura di poemi e saggi in latino. All'età di 22 anni, nel 1694, cominciò anche a mostrare la sua capacità nella poesia in inglese.

Un dettaglio notevole della sua vita che gli comunicò la misericordia di Dio è come riuscì a sfuggire per un soffio a un terribile naufragio. Fu questa tragedia e il suo racconto spaventoso di sopravvivenza che avrebbero ispirato la stesura di questo inno edificante.

Ecco l'inno con le 13 strofe originali:

Quando tutte le Tue misericordie, o mio Dio,
L’anima mia che sorge contempla,
Trasportata dalla vista,
Sono perso in meraviglia, amore e lode.

La Tua Provvidenza sostenne la mia vita,
E provvide a tutti i miei bisogni,
Mentre giacevo nel silenzioso grembo,
E pendevo dal seno.

A tutti i miei deboli lamenti e grida
La Tua misericordia prestò orecchio,
Ancor prima che i miei pensieri fiacchi avessero imparato
A formarsi in preghiera.

Innumerevoli consolazioni all’anima mia
La Tua tenera cura elargì,
Prima che il mio cuore infantile concepisse
Da chi quelle consolazioni fluissero.

Quando nei stradoni scivolosi della giovinezza
Con passi sconsiderati correvo,
Il Tuo braccio invisibile mi trasportò salvo,
E mi guidò fino all’età matura.

Tra pericoli nascosti, fatiche e morti,
Dolce spianò il mio cammino;
E attraverso le piacevoli insidie del vizio,
Più da temere di esse.

O come potranno le parole con egual calore
Dichiarare la gratitudine,
Che brucia dentro il mio cuore rapito?
Ma tu puoi leggerla lì.

La Tua mano generosa con beni mondani
Ha fatto traboccare la mia coppa;
E, in un amico gentile e fedele,
Ha raddoppiato tutto il mio avere.

Diecimila diecimila doni preziosi
Occupano le mie grazie quotidiane;
Né ultimo è un cuore gioioso
Che assapora quei doni con letizia.

Quando stanco per la malattia, spesso Tu
Con salute rinnovasti il mio volto;
E, quando in peccati e dolori sprofondavo,
Rivivesti la mia anima con grazia.

Attraverso ogni periodo della mia vita
Perseguirò la Tua bontà
E dopo la morte, in mondi lontani,
Rinnovare il glorioso tema.

Quando la natura verrà meno, e giorno e notte
Non divideranno più le Tue opere,
Il mio cuore sempre grato,
O Signore, adorerà la Tua misericordia.

Per tutta l’eternità a Te
Eleverò un canto gioioso;
Poiché, oh, l’eternità è troppo breve
Per pronunciare tutta la Tua lode!

Mentre cerchiamo di comprendere la vita e la storia dell’inno, diamo un breve sguardo ad alcune delusioni che egli affrontò. Rimasto celibe fino ai suoi 40 anni, nutriva speranze di avere un giorno un matrimonio felice. Il suo matrimonio con Charlotte, vedova da 15 anni, non si rivelò come aveva anticipato. Si dice che il loro corteggiamento fu lungo e ansioso. Si sposarono nell’agosto del 1716 nel suo 44° anno. Una citazione afferma che “Si dice che la conobbe per la prima volta diventando il tutore di suo figlio. Il matrimonio, se si può dar credito al rapporto non contraddetto, non apportò alcun incremento alla sua felicità; non li trovò né li rese uguali."* Oltre al suo matrimonio meno che ideale, la perdita del suo buon amico Richard Steele qualche tempo dopo lo colpì profondamente.

Verso il 1717 la sua salute cominciò a declinare rapidamente, e nel marzo 1718 dovette dimettersi da alcune sue cariche, avendo grande bisogno di riposo e quiete. “La malattia di cui Addison soffriva appare essere stata l’asma. Divenne più violenta dopo il suo ritiro dall’ufficio ed ora fu accompagnata da idropisia. Il suo letto di morte fu placido e rassegnato, e confortato da quelle speranze religiose che così spesso aveva suggerito agli altri..." *

Un'ultima nota che includo qui sulla vita dell'autore dell'inno è il racconto della sua dipartita. C'era un giovane di nome Lord Warwick, dall'indole rozza e libertina, che Addison aveva spesso cercato di conquistare alla fede, tutto inutilmente. Avvicinandosi alla fine della sua vita, fece un ultimo tentativo per impressionare quel giovane sull'importanza del cristianesimo. Lo fece chiamare per essere presente mentre moriva, dicendo: "Ti ho mandato a chiamare affinché tu possa vedere come può morire un cristiano." Non abbiamo resoconti su come questa esperienza influenzò il comportamento di Warwick, ma possiamo supporre che molto probabilmente lo abbia fatto. Joseph Addison morì a Holland House il 17 giugno 1719, sei settimane dopo il suo 47º compleanno. È sepolto nel Poet's Corner dell'Abbazia di Westminster.

Questo inno ha diverse melodie: “St Peter,” composta da Alexander Robert Reinagle nel 1836, è usata nel Church Hymnal e nel Christian Hymnary. La melodia "Geneva" fu composta da John Cole nel 1805. Egli nacque a Tewksbury, Inghilterra, e venne negli Stati Uniti nella sua fanciullezza. Baltimore, Maryland divenne la sua casa americana, dove fu istruito. Presto nella vita divenne musicista e editore di musica. Continuò a comporre fino alla sua morte. Questa melodia si trova in Zion's Praises, Hymns of the Church e Harmonia Sacra. La melodia "Contemplation", composta da F.A. Gore Ouseley, è più ampiamente usata da gruppi evangelici e altre comunità ecclesiali. Altri inni di Joseph Addison includono "The Lord my Pasture Shall Prepare" e "The Spacious Firmament." Ecco una citazione finale per aiutarci a capire chi era Joseph Addison e cosa credeva. "La sua religione non ha nulla di entusiastico o superstizioso; non appare né debitamente credulone né volontariamente scettico; la sua moralità non è né pericolosamente lassista né impraticabilmente rigorosa. Tutto l'incanto della fantasia e tutta la forza dell'argomentazione sono impiegati per raccomandare al lettore il suo reale interesse, la cura di compiacere l'Autore del suo essere."

*tratto da Wikipedia e hymnary.org

The message was brief. “Dr. Waldron, would you call Mrs. Jones back about her labs?”

I was puzzled. I didn’t remember ordering any labs for Mrs. Jones. As far as I could remember, she was seeing a specialist and just had surgery for colon cancer. Maybe they had ordered the labs. But if so, they certainly should have followed up on them.

I opened the chart and looked in the lab section. Quickly my eye went to my patient’s kidney function and stopped. Her kidney function had declined a huge amount in the last week.

I called her and then her kidney specialist. Over the next half hour, her situation came into view. Because of her colon surgery, she was losing a lot of fluid, enough that she couldn’t keep up. This, in turn, was making her kidney function a lot worse, along with dropping her potassium level.

To take care of it, she would need IV fluids – once or twice a week – to keep up with the fluids she was losing. Without that, her kidneys would shut down completely.

In a sense, Mrs. Jones was dealing with kidney burnout—a situation where they were putting out more than they were taking in and suffering as a result.

As I was thinking about this, my mind went to the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea is “Dead” because it has such a high level of minerals and salts that very few, other than a few microorganisms, can survive.

The reason for this is that the Dead Sea has no outlet. The Jordan River drains into it, carrying fresh water, and then sits in a basin. Some of the water evaporates, and what remains are the salts and minerals in the water.

Over the thousands of years since the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah, this inland body of water has become one of the saltiest places on earth. It is a body of water that is neither useful for irrigation nor a place where plants and animals can thrive.

Neither situation is healthy, yet this is exactly how most people live their lives, typically gravitating towards one pole or the other. Either they fill their schedule to the maximum, leaving no time for quiet reflection, or they resist any efforts to get them to invest their time and talents and avoid these sorts of activities.

I want to spend a little time thinking about burnout. What causes it, and how we can avoid it?

Everyone has Limits

I Samuel 30 tells the story of David returning to Ziklag. Upon his arrival, he discovered, to his dismay, that the Amalekites had invaded Philistine territory, burned the town, and taken captive all the people who were present.

David and his men had been gone three days and were already tired from their journey to and from Aphek, where King Agag had mustered his forces. Despite this and their anguish at the loss of their family members and material possessions, David consulted God and decided to pursue to the Amalekites out into the desert.

They had only gone as far as the Brook Besor when a third of his men gave up. Scripture tells us they were “too faint” to cross the brook. They were physically and mentally exhausted. Even if they had been able to hold things together for another day, they would be useless in battle.

So it was that David left them behind and continued to pursue the Amalekites, eventually defeating them with the four hundred men who were able to persevere. Here, we come to the interesting part. The men who had won the victory looked down on the men who had been faint. They said those faint-hearted men could have their families back, but all the spoil would be reserved for those who had won the victory.

In response, David said, “Ye shall not do so, my brethren, with that which the Lord hath given us, who hath preserved us, and delivered the company that came against us into our hand. For who will hearken unto you in this matter? but as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff: they shall part alike.” (I Samuel 30:23,24)

David did not wish to penalize those who had tried but did not have the strength to make it through to the final battle.

Perhaps this speaks of the grace we ought to extend to others who don’t have the strength or energy to continue for a season. Maybe it lets us know that we should extend that same grace to ourselves.

What is Burnout?

There are different definitions for burnout, but it all comes down to a state of physical, mental, or emotional exhaustion related to too much stress over an extended period of time. We tend to think of this stress as work-related. There are too many projects going on at once, not enough help, or an employer who has high expectations.

Stress is stress, and it all adds up. Even if work isn’t stressful, if you have a newborn baby at home, a family member with dementia, or many church responsibilities, you can still reach the place where you have little left to give.

It is as though you are in a vehicle traveling 90 mph, and you push the accelerator a little harder, and nothing happens. In response, you push the gas pedal even harder, and a screeching noise comes from the engine. Suddenly, the dashboard lights up with funny lights, and the car starts to slow down.

The question is, how can we avoid burnout and what should we do if we realize that we are heading towards it?

Understanding Burnout

Burnout leads to both physical and emotional depletion. The problem with burnout is that even if a particular stressor causes it – say, a situation at work or a family health problem – it will affect numerous other relationships.

People dealing with burnout often exhibit symptoms consistent with depression and anxiety. They may become withdrawn, lack motivation to be involved with church and family activities, or get angry quicker than people who are not dealing with burnout.

There is even a suggestion that burnout can lead to the weakening of our immune systems. This could lead to more colds and viral infections.

Identify Early Signs

We need to know ourselves. There are signs that other people can see in our lives and how we relate to others that we don’t necessarily identify as a problem.

People who are on the edge of burnout feel hopeless. They may hide it from their coworkers, but often, their family members realize that something is wrong. You used to have a sunny disposition, and now you are discouraged, not only about the present but also the future.

You might lack motivation and have low energy levels. In a sense, you are going through the motions and just doing enough to get by – both at work and in your home. This is likely related to your feelings of hopelessness.

You may find that you are more irritable than you used to be. Little things bother or aggravate you, and you find yourself smothering angry retorts.

It is important to realize that you are heading down this road for several reasons. First, you are not the only one who suffers when you are burned out. Your family must deal with you and your “grumpiness.” Also, the longer you go without taking care of things, the harder it is to get back to a place of balance.

As a physician, I see people all the time who “didn’t have time” to get something taken care of until they could no longer ignore it. At this point, it will take a major procedure to set things right. It would have been easier to correct if they came in with the first symptom.

Make a Priority List

Everything in our life has a priority level. People who do not prioritize end up feeling scattered as they try to do everything at once. This is a recipe for disaster. To me, it makes sense to divide our tasks into four buckets:

  1. Things that need to be done relatively quickly
  2. Things that need to be done but can wait a bit
  3. Things that we’d like to do, but don’t need to
  4. Things that we should let go of.

Here might be a good place to mention that just because something needs to be done does not mean you need to do it. Sometimes, someone in your home or workplace could help with one of the tasks on your to-do list.

Once we have made our priority list, we need to do something about it. If you simply assign a priority to everything in your life but continue to try to do everything, it won’t help your situation at all.

The point of this exercise is to figure out what things you can eliminate from your schedule, so you have more space to breathe.

Make First Things First

One of the things that happens when we are overwhelmed is that we stop doing self-care. We grab unhealthy food on the go, stop spending time in prayer and devotions, and quit exercising.

Doing these things takes time, and that is exactly what we think we don’t have when we are living on the margins of our energy. Self-care is extremely important but often gets assigned a priority of zero and is seldom included in a day’s activity.

As we begin to replenish our spiritual nourishment, we must also make sure we take care of our physical health.

Take Time Apart

After feeding the multitudes, Mark 6:46 tells of Jesus, “And when he had sent them away, he departed into a mountain to pray.” Even Jesus had times when He needed to be alone without distractions.

It is easy to focus on the prayer aspect of this passage, and that is important, but let's focus on the solitary aspect of this experience. Jesus even left His closest followers behind during this time of seeking God’s face.

There are times when we need to escape from the pressure of human interactions and find a peaceful place where we can be alone.

Put Down Technology

Part of making rest time truly restful is to eliminate sources of distraction. Phones and electronic tablets are exactly the types of things that can keep our minds from achieving the peace (shalom) that we both desire and need.

Digital burnout is a new term that is being used to describe people who feel apathetic and exhausted from spending hours each day staring at screens. Many workers spend seven or eight hours a day looking at computer screens and then get even more screen time after work.

The funny thing is that the most productive workers are often people who use old-fashioned things like paper calendars and leave phones out of meetings. As wonderful as phones are, they are also immensely distracting for most of us.

So often, we have time away that is simply not restful. The reason is that we continue to receive texts and emails and can still access social media. If you are not someone who can put his phone away and ignore it (it takes a lot of willpower to do this), then leave your phone in another room and create some distance. This will seem stressful, but we can focus on recharging ourselves by creating a screen-free zone.

Build Breaks into Your Day

There is a certain amount of work that must be done each day, and it often feels like too much for the allotted 24 hours. There is certainly no time to stop, stretch, and take a five-minute walk, or at least that's what we tell ourselves.

In reality, if you take a five-minute break every few hours to do something non-work related, you will come back refreshed and more ready to deal with the problems of the day.

Do something healthy during this time. Take a short walk or eat an apple. Chowing down a bag of potato chips or eating a couple candy bars is not likely to produce the desired results.

The problem is often with our own expectations. People who struggle with burnout often have extremely high personal standards and get frustrated when they not measure up to that standard.

Be Intentional about Rest

One of the messages of the Old Testament was the importance of the Sabbath. I have heard many people argue that in the New Testament period, we no longer need to practice the Sabbath. Didn’t Paul say that one day was like the other? Didn’t Jesus defend His disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath?

Regardless of what you believe about the importance of keeping the Sabbath, it is still important that we take time to rest. This is the real message that Jesus was conveying when He said that the “Sabbath was created for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Rest is not simply sleeping till 10 am and then doing nothing. Rest is actively making decisions that will help us recharge our depleted batteries. Go out for breakfast with a friend, take a hike, or take a good book and go somewhere without cell service and focus on something other than situations that are depleting you.

Jesus understood the human need for rest, this is why He told His disciples “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). This time of rest would give them energy for their next time of ministry.

Don’t Buy into Myths

People tell themselves all sorts of lies that can lead to pushing themselves too hard. I’ll list a few of them and some thoughts about each one.

“I’m the only one who can do this task.” This feels true. The other people in our home or workplace are not helping us the way we wish that they would. Sometimes, it simply feels easier to do the task ourselves rather than spend time teaching someone else how to do it. We need to remember that if we died, the people around us would figure out how to get things done. We can assign them some of the tasks today before we die.

“If I just get this job done today, tomorrow will be easier.” I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but each day has 24 hours, and somehow, they always get filled up. I have given up the idea that there is a time in my life coming up soon that will have nothing on the schedule. If a rest comes, it will come because I have made an effort to clear my schedule, not because by some random occurrence, one day, I happen to not have a single task in it.

“God will never give me more than I can handle.” God has promised many things. He has promised that when there is a temptation, He will give us an opportunity to escape it (I Corinthians 10:13). He has also promised that He will never leave us or forsake us (Hebrews 13:5). I do not read anywhere in Scripture that God will keep us from overfilling our lives. He has simply promised that He will give us opportunity to take a different path and will walk beside us on our way.

So often the heavy load we carry is because other people, or even we, ourselves, have put too many things on our task list. Suppose I choose to put too many patients on my schedule and I am feeling exhausted. In that case, it is time for me to take responsibility for what I have done, rather than claiming a mythical promise that God will keep me from overwhelming myself.

“These are all good things that I am doing.” Doctors face this a lot. We want to squeeze one more patient into the schedule and stay just a little later to answer another message because we feel responsible. We hate to think that someone might need to go to the Emergency Department because we did not take care of them when they needed help.

Just because the things in your schedule are “good things” that benefit other people and are building the kingdom, does not mean that you don’t need to cut back in one area or another. If you are feeling emotionally depleted, it is probably time to remove a few items from your to-do list.

Conclusion

There are other things that could be mentioned. Getting support from someone else, meditating on Scripture, and even taking a vacation are all things that can help.

When I read about some of the famous preachers of the past, I see in some of their lives a roller coaster. They pushed themselves to the max, got involved in large numbers of projects, and then had an emotional breakdown. They would take some time off and, a month or two later, launch back into the same activities. This cycle continued for their whole ministry.

Jesus tells us that His yoke is easy, and His burden is light (Matt, 11:28-30). If we are at the point of exhaustion, we need to consider whether we have Jesus’ yoke or if we are laboring under the burden of our own creation.

Jesus knows our limitations. He wants us to have balance, living in such a way that we not only have strength for today but also for tomorrow, next week, and next year – till He comes again.

كانت الرسالة موجزة. «دكتور والدْرون، هل تتصل بالسيدة جونز لإخبارها بنتائج تحاليلها؟»

شعرت بالحيرة. لم أتذكر أنني طلبت أي تحاليل للسيدة جونز. على حد ما أتذكر، كانت تراجع أخصائياً وخضعت لتوها لعملية استئصال سرطان القولون. ربما هم من طلبوا التحاليل. لكن لو كان الأمر كذلك، فينبغي بالتأكيد أن يكونوا قد تابَعوا النتائج.

فتحت السجل ونظرت إلى قسم المختبرات. بسرعة توقفت عيناي عند وظيفة الكلى لدى مريضي. لقد تدهورت وظيفة كليتها بشكل كبير خلال الأسبوع الماضي.

اتصلت بها ثم بأخصائي الكلى. خلال نصف ساعة، تجلّت لي الصورة. بسبب عملية القولون كانت تفقد الكثير من السوائل، بما لا تستطيع تعويضه. وهذا بدوره كان يجعل وظيفة كليتيها تسوء كثيراً، مع انخفاض مستوى البوتاسيوم لديها.

للعناية بذلك، كانت بحاجة إلى سوائل وريدية — مرة أو مرتين في الأسبوع — لمواكبة ما تفقده من سوائل. من دون ذلك ستتوقف كليتاها تمامًا.

من ناحية ما، كانت السيدة جونز تعاني من احتراق كلوي — حالة تبذل فيها الكليتان أكثر مما تستقبلان فتتأذيان نتيجةً لذلك.

وأثناء تفكيري في ذلك، انتقل ذهني إلى البحر الميت. البحر الميت «ميت» لأن نسبة المعادن والأملاح فيه عالية جداً فلا يمكن لمعظم الكائنات، سوى بعض الميكروبات، أن تبقى فيه.

سبب ذلك أن البحر الميت لا منفذ له. نهر الأردن يصبُّ فيه حاملاً ماءً عذباً ثم يجلس في حوض داخلي. يتبخر بعض الماء، وما يتبقى هي الأملاح والمعادن في الماء.

على مدى آلاف السنين منذ سقوط سدوم وعمورة، أصبح هذا المسطح المائي الداخلى من أكثر الأماكن ملوحةً على وجه الأرض. إنه جسم مائي لا يصلح للري ولا مكاناً تنمو فيه النباتات أو تزدهر الحيوانات.

لا حالتا الأمور صحيحتان، ومع ذلك هكذا يعيش معظم الناس حياتهم، يميلون عادة إلى أحد القطبين أو الآخر. إما أن يملأوا جدولهم إلى الحد الأقصى فلا يبقى وقت للتأمل الهادئ، أو أنهم يقاومون أي جهد لدفعهم لاستثمار وقتهم ومواهبهم ويتجنبون مثل هذه الأنشطة.

أود أن أقضي بعض الوقت في التفكير في الاحتراق. ما الذي يسببه، وكيف يمكن أن نتجنبه؟

لكل إنسان حدود

تُخبرنا قصة صموئيل الأول 30 عن عودة داود إلى صِقلاق. عند وصوله اكتشف — لخيبة أمله — أن الْعَمَاليق غزوا أرض الفلسطينيين وأحرقوا المدينة وأسروا كل الناس الذين كانوا فيها.

كان داود ورجاله قد غادروا ثلاثة أيام وكانوا متعبين بالفعل من رحلتهم ذهاباً وإياباً إلى عِفق حيث حشد الملك آغاق قواته. بالرغم من ذلك وحزنهم على فقدان أهلهم وممتلكاتهم، استشار داود الربّ وقرر أن يطارد الْعَمَاليق إلى البريّة.

لم يقطعوا مسافة طويلة حتى غدر بِصر، إذ استسلم ثلث رجاله. تخبرنا الآيات أنهم «أضعفوا» عن عبور الوادي. كانوا مرهقين جسدياً وذهنياً. حتى لو استمروا ليوم آخر لما كانوا ليكونوا نافعين في القتال.

فتركهم داود واستمر في المطاردة وهزم الْعَمَاليق بالأخير مع الأربعمئة رجل الذين استطاعوا الصمود. وهنا الجزء المثير للاهتمام. الرجال الذين حققوا النصر احتقروا الرجال الذين أضعفهم التعب. قالوا أن أولئك الضعفاء يمكنهم استرجاع أسرهم، لكن الغنيمة تُحجز لمن نال النصر.

فردّ داود قائلاً: «لا تفعلون هكذا يا إخوتي تجاه ما أعطانا الربّ، الذي حفظنا وأسلم الجماعة التي قامت علينا بيدنا. فمن يسمع إليكم في هذا الأمر؟ بل كما نصيب ذاك الخارج إلى الحرب، هكذا نصيب ذلك القائم عند الغنيمة: يقتسمون معاً.» (صموئيل الأول 30:23،24)

لم يرغب داود في معاقبة الذين حاولوا ولكن لم تكن لديهم القوة لإكمال المشهد حتى المعركة النهائية.

ربما يشير هذا إلى النعمة التي يجب أن نمنحها للآخرين الذين لا تهيئهم القوة أو الطاقة للاستمرار لموسم ما. وربما يذكرنا أننا يجب أن نمنح هذه النعمة لأنفسنا أيضاً.

ما هو الاحتراق؟

تختلف التعاريف للاحتراق، لكنه كله يعود إلى حالة من الاستنزاف الجسدي أو الذهني أو العاطفي المرتبطة بضغط طويل الأمد. نميل إلى اعتبار هذا الضغط مرتبطاً بالعمل: مشاريع كثيرة في آن واحد، مساعدة غير كافية، أو رب عمل يتوقع الكثير.

الضغط هو ضغط، ويتراكم. حتى لو لم يكن العمل مجهدًا، فإذا كان لديك مولود حديث في المنزل، أو أحد أفراد الأسرة يعاني من الخرف، أو مسؤوليات كثيرة في الكنيسة، يمكنك أن تبلغ نقطة لا يبقى لديك ما تعطيه.

يشبه الأمر أن تكون في مركبة تسير بسرعة 90 ميلاً في الساعة ثم تضغط دواسة الوقود بقوة فلا يحدث شيء. فتضغطها أكثر فيصدر عن المحرك صرير. فجأة تضيء لوحة العدّادات بأنوار غريبة وتبدأ السيارة في التباطؤ.

السؤال هو: كيف نتجنّب الاحتراق، وما الذي ينبغي أن نفعله إذا أدركنا أننا في طريقنا نحوه؟

فهم الاحتراق

الاحتراق يؤدي إلى استنزاف جسدي وعاطفي على حد سواء. المشكلة أن الاحتراق، حتى لو سببه عامل ضاغط محدد — مثلاً وضع في العمل أو مشكلة صحية في الأسرة — فإنه يؤثر على علاقات كثيرة أخرى.

أشخاص يعانون من الاحتراق غالباً ما تظهر عليهم أعراض متسقة مع الاكتئاب والقلق. قد يصبحون منطويين، يفقدون الدافع للمشاركة في أنشطة الكنيسة والأسرة، أو يغضبون أسرع من غيرهم الذين لا يواجهون الاحتراق.

هناك أيضاً اقتراح بأن الاحتراق قد يؤدي إلى إضعاف جهاز المناعة. وهذا قد يؤدي إلى نزلات برد وعدوى فيروسية أكثر.

التعرّف على العلامات المبكّرة

نحتاج أن نعرف أنفسنا. هناك علامات يمكن للآخرين أن يروا في حياتنا وفي تعاملنا مع الآخرين قد لا نُدركها نحن كمشكلة.

من هم على حافة الاحتراق يشعرون باليأس. قد يخفون ذلك عن زملائهم في العمل، لكن غالباً ما يلاحظ أفراد الأسرة أن هناك خطباً ما. كنت تتمتع بمزاج مشرق، والآن أنت محبط، ليس فقط بشأن الحاضر بل أيضاً بشأن المستقبل.

قد تفتقر إلى الدافع وتصبح مستويات طاقتك منخفضة. إلى حد ما، تكون تمشي على الروتين وتؤدي الحد الأدنى لتتماسك — سواء في العمل أو في المنزل. وترتبط هذه الحالة غالباً بمشاعر اليأس.

قد تكتشف أنك أكثر تهيّجاً مما كنت عليه سابقاً. أشياء صغيرة تزعجك أو تثيرك، وتجد نفسك كاتماً لردود فعل غاضبة.

من المهم أن تدرك أنك تسير في هذا الطريق لعدة أسباب. أولاً، أنت لست الوحيد المتألم عندما تكون محروقاً؛ عائلتك تضطر إلى التعامل معك ومع «تجهمك». كذلك، كلما طالت المدة دون أن تعتني بالأمر، أصبح من الأصعب العودة إلى حالة توازن.

كطبيب، أرى الناس طوال الوقت الذين «لم يكن لديهم وقت» ليعتنوا بأمر ما إلى أن لم يعودوا قادرين على تجاهله. في هذه المرحلة، سيتطلب الأمر إجراءً كبيراً لتصحيح المسار. كان من الأسهل تصحيح الوضع لو جاؤوا عند ظهور العَرَض الأول.

ضع قائمة أولويات

كل شيء في حياتنا له مستوى أولوية. الأشخاص الذين لا يُعطون أولوية ينتهون بشعور التشتت بينما يحاولون فعل كل شيء دفعة واحدة. هذه وصفة لكارثة. بالنسبة لي، من المفيد تقسيم مهامنا إلى أربع دلاء:

  1. أمور يجب إنجازها بسرعة نسبياً
  2. أمور يجب إنجازها لكن يمكن تأجيلها قليلاً
  3. أمور نود فعلها، لكن لا نحتاج إليها
  4. أمور يجب أن نتخلى عنها.

هنا من المناسب أن أذكر أن مجرد أن شيئاً ما يجب فعله لا يعني أنك مضطر لفعله بنفسك. أحياناً شخص في منزلك أو مكان عملك يمكنه المساعدة في إحدى مهام قائمة الأعمال.

بعد أن نعد قائمة أولوياتنا، علينا أن نفعل شيئاً بشأنها. إذا اكتفيت بتعيين أولوية لكل شيء في حياتك لكن واصلت محاولة القيام بكل شيء بنفسك، فلن يساعد ذلك موقفك أبداً.

هدف هذا التمرين هو معرفة الأشياء التي يمكنك إزالتها من جدولك لتترك مساحة أكبر للتنفّس.

ضع الأمور الأولى أولاً

من الأمور التي تحدث عندما نكون مرهقين أننا نتوقف عن الاعتناء بأنفسنا. نلتقط طعاماً غير صحي أثناء التنقّل، نتوقف عن قضاء وقت في الصلاة والتأمل، ونكف عن ممارسة الرياضة.

أداء هذه الأمور يتطلب وقتاً، وهذا بالضبط ما نعتقد أننا لا نملكه عندما نعيش على هامش طاقتنا. الاعتناء بالنفس مهم للغاية لكنه غالباً ما يحتل أولوية صفر ونادراً ما يُدرَج في نشاطات اليوم.

بينما نبدأ في تجديد غذائنا الروحي، يجب أيضاً أن نضمن أننا نعتني بصحتنا الجسدية.

خذ وقتاً للانفراد

بعد إطعام الجموع، يخبرنا مرقس 6:46 عن يسوع: «ولما أَرسلهم، ارتحل إلى الجبل ليصلي.» حتى يسوع كانت له أوقات يحتاج فيها إلى أن يكون وحيداً بلا مشتتات.

من السهل التركيز على جانب الصلاة في هذه الآية، وهذا مهم، لكن دعونا نركز على جانب الانفراد في هذه التجربة. ترك يسوع حتى أقرب أتباعه في هذا الوقت وهو يسعى لوجه الله.

هناك أوقات نحتاج فيها إلى الهروب من ضغط التفاعلات البشرية ونجد مكاناً هادئاً نكون فيه بمفردنا.

اترك التكنولوجيا جانباً

جزء من جعل وقت الراحة فعلاً راحة هو إقصاء مصادر التشتت. الهواتف والأجهزة اللوحية الإلكترونية هي بالضبط الأشياء التي قد تمنع عقولنا من بلوغ السلام (شالوم) الذي نريده ونحتاجه.

الاحتراق الرقمي مصطلح جديد يُستخدم لوصف الأشخاص الذين يشعرون باللامبالاة والإرهاق من قضاء ساعات يومياً أمام الشاشات. كثير من العاملين يقضون سبع أو ثماني ساعات يومياً أمام شاشات الحاسوب ثم يحصلون على مزيد من وقت الشاشة بعد العمل.

الغريب أن أكثر العمال إنتاجية هم غالباً من يستخدمون وسائل قديمة مثل مفكرات ورقية ويتركون الهواتف خارج الاجتماعات. ورغم روعة الهواتف، فهي أيضاً مشتتة للغاية بالنسبة لغالبية الناس.

كثيراً ما يكون لدينا وقت بعيد لكنه ليس مُرتاحاً ببساطة لأننا نستمر في استقبال الرسائل القصيرة والبريد الإلكتروني ويمكننا الوصول إلى وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي. إن لم تكن من الأشخاص القادرين على وضع هاتفه جانباً وتجاهله (فهذا يتطلب قوة إرادة كبيرة)، فاترك هاتفك في غرفة أخرى واصنع بعض المسافة. سيبدو هذا مرهقاً في البداية، لكن يمكننا التركيز على إعادة شحن أنفسنا بخلق منطقة خالية من الشاشات.

أدر فترات راحة ضمن يومك

هناك قدر من العمل يجب أن يُنجز كل يوم، وغالباً ما يبدو أنه أكثر مما تسمح به الأربع وعشرون ساعة. بالتأكيد لا وقت للتوقف والتمدد والمشي مدة خمس دقائق، أو هذا ما نقوله لأنفسنا على الأقل.

في الواقع، إذا أخذت استراحة قصيرة كل بضع ساعات لتقوم بشيء غير متعلق بالعمل، فستعود منتعشاً وأكثر استعداداً للتعامل مع مشكلات اليوم.

قم بشيء صحي خلال هذا الوقت. تمشّ قليلاً أو تناول تفاحة. التهام كيس رقائق بطاطس أو قضمتين من لوحين شوكولاتة على الأرجح لن يعطي النتائج المرجوة.

المشكلة غالباً في توقعاتنا نحن أنفسنا. الأشخاص الذين يكافحون مع الاحتراق عادة ما يكون لديهم معايير شخصية عالية جداً ويغضبون عندما لا يرقون إلى تلك المعايير.

كن متعمداً في الراحة

واحدة من رسائل العهد القديم كانت أهمية السبت. سمعت كثيرين يجادلون أنه في العهد الجديد لم نعد بحاجة إلى ممارسة السبت. ألم يقل بولس أن يوماً كاليوم الآخر؟ ألم يدافع يسوع عن تلاميذه لقطف السنابل في السبت؟

بغض النظر عما تعتقده بشأن أهمية حفظ السبت، يبقى أنه من المهم أن نأخذ وقتاً للراحة. هذه هي الرسالة الحقيقية التي كان يسوع يقصدها حين قال إن «السبت وُضع للإنسان لا الإنسان للسبت» (مرقس 2:27).

الراحة ليست مجرد النوم حتى العاشرة صباحاً ثم عدم فعل شيء. الراحة هي اتخاذ قرارات فاعلة تساعدنا على إعادة شحن بطارياتنا المستنزفة. اخرج لتناول الفطور مع صديق، اذهب للتنزه، أو خذ كتاباً جيداً واذهب إلى مكان بلا تغطية خلوية وركّز على شيء غير الحالات التي تستنزفك.

فهم يسوع حاجة الإنسان للراحة، ولهذا قال لتلاميذه: «تعالوا أنتم المنفردون إلى موضع خلاء وارتحوا قليلاً» (مرقس 6:31). هذه الفترة من الراحة كانت ستمنحهم طاقة لخدمتهم القادمة.

لا تقبل الأساطير

يخدع الناس أنفسهم بأقوالٍ قد تدفعهم للمبالغة في الجهد. سأذكر بعضها مع أفكار عن كل واحد منها.

«أنا الوحيد الذي يستطيع إنجاز هذه المهمة.» هذا الشعور يبدو حقيقياً. الآخرون في منزلنا أو مكان عملنا لا يساعدوننا كما نريد. أحياناً يبدو أسهل أن نفعل المهمة بأنفسنا بدل قضاء وقت في تعليم غيرنا. يجب أن نتذكر أنه لو متّ، سيجد الناس من حولنا طريقة لإنجاز الأمور. يمكننا أن نُسند بعض المهام اليوم قبل أن نموت.

«إذا أنجزت هذه المهمة اليوم، سيكون الغد أسهل.» أكره أن أكون ناقل أخبار سيئة، لكن كل يوم له أربع وعشرون ساعة وبطريقة ما تمتلئ دائماً. تخلّيت عن فكرة أن هناك وقتاً قادماً في حياتي سيكون جدولي فيه فارغاً تماماً. إن أتت راحة، فستأتي لأنني بذلت جهداً لتنظيف جدولي، لا لأن حدثاً عشوائياً جعل يوماً دون مهمة على الإطلاق.

«لن يعطيني الله أكثر مما أستطيع تحمّله.» الله وعد بأمور كثيرة. وعد أنه حين تأتي تجربة سيعطينا مخرجاً منها (1 كورنثوس 10:13). كما وعد أنه لا يتركنا ولا يهجرنا (عبرانيين 13:5). لا أقرأ في الكتاب المقدس أن الله سيمنعنا من ملء حياتنا زيادة على طاقتها. لقد وعد ببساطة أن يمنحنا فرصة أن نسلك طريقاً مختلفاً وسيَسِرَ معنا في الطريق.

غالباً ما يكون الحمل الثقيل الذي نحمله نتيجة أن الآخرين، أو حتى نحن أنفسنا، وضعوا الكثير من الأمور في قائمة مهامنا. لو اخترت أن أضع الكثير من المرضى في جدولي وأشعر بالإرهاق، فقد حان الوقت لأتحمل مسؤولية ما فعلته بدلاً من ادعاء وعد أسطوري بأن الله سيمنعني من إرهاق نفسي.

«كل هذه الأشياء جيدة التي أفعلها.» يواجه الأطباء هذا كثيراً. نريد أن نضيف مريضاً آخر إلى الجدول ونبقى قليلاً للإجابة على رسالة لأننا نشعر بالمسؤولية. نكره أن نفكر أن شخصاً ما قد يحتاج للذهاب إلى قسم الطوارئ لأننا لم نعتن به عندما احتاج للمساعدة.

فقط لأن الأشياء في جدولك «أشياء جيدة» تنفع الآخرين وتبني الملكوت، فهذا لا يعني أنك لا تحتاج لتقليل شيء ما أو آخر. إذا كنت تشعر باستنزاف عاطفي، فربما حان الوقت لإزالة بعض البنود من قائمة مهامك.

الخاتمة

هناك أمور أخرى يمكن ذكرها. الحصول على دعم من شخص آخر، التأمل في الكتاب المقدس، وحتى أخذ إجازة كلها أشياء مفيدة.

عندما أقرأ عن بعض الوعاظ المشهورين في الماضي، أرى في حياتهم أحياناً دوامة صعود وهبوط. دفعوا أنفسهم إلى الحد الأقصى، انخرطوا في عدد كبير من المشاريع، ثم انهاروا عاطفياً. كانوا يأخذون استراحة ثم بعد شهر أو شهرين يعودون إلى نفس الأنشطة. استمر هذا النمط طوال فترة خدمتهم.

يخبرنا يسوع أن نيره مريح وحمله خفيف (متّى 11:28-30). إذا كنا عند نقطة الإرهاق، يجب أن نفكر هل نتحمل نير يسوع أم أننا نعمل تحت عبء صنعناه بأنفسنا.

يسوع يعرف حدودنا. يريدنا أن نكون متوازنين، نعيش بطريقة تمنحنا القوة ليس فقط لليوم بل لغد، والأسبوع القادم، والسنة القادمة — حتى يأتي مجدداً.

"O give thanks unto the God of heaven: for His mercy endureth for ever"
—Psalm 136:26

In your journey of life, from infancy to where you are today, have you ever taken a few minutes to meditate on the mercy God has shown you? Infancy to childhood, childhood to youth, youth to adulthood, and beyond, God's everlasting mercy is upon them that fear Him! The scripture says in Deuteronomy 7:9 that the mercy of God extends way past our short lives here on earth, even to a thousand generations. Take a moment and wonder in the glory and beauty of this unchanging, eternal attribute of God!

As we take a look at the history behind this hymn, let us endeavor to see the hand of God at work in the life of the hymn writer. The hymn, "When All Thy Mercies O My God," written in 1712, has been published in 994 hymnals and is to this day in the list of the best 100 hymns ever written. As the writer nears the end of his time on earth, he reflects in this hymn his awe at the mercies of God toward him throughout his life.

Joseph Addison, born May 1, 1672, was an English essayist, poet, and man of letters. Concerning his birth, we find that he “appeared weak and unlikely to live", Mr. Tyers says.* And that “he was laid out for dead as soon as he was born.” Without doubt, the providence of God preserved his young life and gave him nearly half a century to serve Him on the earth. He was the eldest son of Lancelot Addison, a well-learned man and minister in his church. His father, being a studious man himself, made sure his son Joseph had a good education. He commenced his studies in his hometown of Milston, in Wiltshire, England.

While in school around 1685, the 13-year-old hymn writer met and became best of friends with Richard Steele, the two of them being only a few months apart in age. They continued their friendship throughout the years, and 27 years later from 1711 to 1712, they cofounded The Spectator magazine, in which this hymn was first published.

After passing through several schools, Addison went to Oxford when he was about 15 years old. While he was there, he continued to gain in learning and skill, especially in the areas of writing Latin poems and essays. By the time he was 22, in 1694, he also began to show his skill at writing English poetry.

One of the most notable details of his life that conveyed to him the mercy of God is how he managed to narrowly escape an awful shipwreck. It was this tragedy and his frightening tale of survival that would go on to inspire the writing of this uplifting hymn.

Here is the hymn with the original 13 verses:

When all Thy mercies, O my God,
My rising soul surveys,
Transported with the view,
I’m lost In wonder, love and praise.

Thy Providence my life sustained,
And all my wants redressed,
While in the silent womb I lay,
And hung upon the breast.

To all my weak complaints and cries
Thy mercy lent an ear,
Ere yet my feeble thoughts had learned,
To form themselves in prayer.

Unnumbered comforts to my soul
Thy tender care bestowed,
Before my infant heart conceived
From Whom those comforts flowed.

When in the slippery paths of youth
With heedless steps I ran,
Thine arm unseen conveyed me safe,
And led me up to man.

Through hidden dangers, toils, and deaths,
It gently cleared my way;
And through the pleasing snares of vice,
More to be feared than they.

O how shall words with equal warmth
The gratitude declare,
That glows within my ravished heart?
But thou canst read it there.

Thy bounteous hand with worldly bliss
Hath made my cup run o’er;
And, in a kind and faithful Friend,
Hath doubled all my store.

Ten thousand thousand precious gifts
My daily thanks employ;
Nor is the last a cheerful heart
That tastes those gifts with joy.

When worn with sickness, oft hast Thou
With health renewed my face;
And, when in sins and sorrows sunk,
Revived my soul with grace.

Through every period of my life
Thy goodness I’ll pursue
And after death, in distant worlds,
The glorious theme renew.

When nature fails, and day and night
Divide Thy works no more,
My ever grateful heart,
O Lord,Thy mercy shall adore.

Through all eternity to Thee
A joyful song I’ll raise;
For, oh, eternity’s too short
To utter all Thy praise!

As we endeavor to understand the life and story of the hymnologist, let's take a short look at some disappointments he faced. Being single into his 40s, he had hopes of someday having a happy marriage. His marriage to Charlotte, a widow of 15 years, didn’t turn out as he had anticipated. It is said that their courtship was long and anxious. They were married in August 1716 in his 44th year. A quote states that “He is said to have first known her by becoming tutor to her son. The marriage, if uncontradicted report can be credited, made no addition to his happiness; it neither found them nor made them equal."* In addition to his less-than-ideal marriage, the loss of his good friend Richard Steele sometime after that took a toll on him.

By the year 1717, his health began to decline rapidly, and by March 1718, he had to resign some of his work positions, having a great need for rest and quietness. "The disease under which Addison laboured appears to have been asthma. It became more violent after his retirement from office and was now accompanied by dropsy. His deathbed was placid and resigned, and comforted by those religious hopes which he had so often suggested to others..." *

One last note I will include here on the life of the hymn writer is the account of his passing. There was a young man by the name of Lord Warwick, rough and loose in character, who Addison had often tried to win to the faith, all to no avail. Nearing the end of his life, he endeavored one last attempt to impress this young man with the importance of Christianity. He sent for him to come and be present as he passed away, saying, "I have sent for you that you may see how a Christian can die." We have no record of how this experience affected Warwick’s behavior, but we can assume that it most likely did. Joseph Addison died at Holland House on the 17th of June, 1719, six weeks after his 47th birthday. He is buried in the Poet's Corner of Westminster Abbey.

This hymn has several tunes: “St Peter,” composed by Alexander Robert Reinagle in 1836, is used in the Church Hymnal and Christian Hymnary. The tune "Geneva" was composed by John Cole in 1805. He was born in Tewksbury, England, and came to the United States in his boyhood. Baltimore, Maryland became his American home, and he was educated there. Early in life, he became a musician and music publisher. He continued to compose music until his death. This tune is found in the Zion's Praises, Hymns of the Church, and Harmonia Sacra. The tune "Contemplation", composed by F.A.Gore Ouseley, is more widely used by evangelical and other church groups. Other hymns by Joseph Addison include "The Lord my Pasture Shall Prepare" and "The Spacious Firmament." Here is one final quote to help us understand who Joseph Addison was and what he believed. "His religion has nothing in it enthusiastic or superstitious; he appears neither weakly credulous nor wantonly skeptical; his morality is neither dangerously lax nor impracticably rigid. All the enchantment of fancy and all the cogency of argument are employed to recommend to the reader his real interest, the care of pleasing the Author of his being."

*sourced from Wikipedia and hymnary.org

"Dá graças ao Deus dos céus: porque a sua misericórdia dura para sempre"
—Salmo 136:26

Na sua jornada de vida, desde a infância até onde está hoje, já tomou alguns minutos para meditar na misericórdia que Deus lhe tem mostrado? Desde o berço até a infância, da infância à juventude, da juventude à vida adulta e além, a misericórdia eterna de Deus está sobre os que O temem! A Escritura diz em Deuteronômio 7:9 que a misericórdia de Deus se estende muito além de nossas curtas vidas aqui na terra, até mil gerações. Reserve um momento e maravilhe-se da glória e da beleza desse atributo imutável e eterno de Deus!

Ao examinarmos a história por trás deste hino, empenhemo-nos em ver a mão de Deus operando na vida do compositor do hino. O hino, "Quando Todas as Tuas Misericórdias, Ó meu Deus", escrito em 1712, foi publicado em 994 hinários e até hoje figura na lista dos 100 melhores hinos já escritos. À medida que o autor se aproxima do fim de seu tempo na terra, ele reflete neste hino sua admiração pelas misericórdias de Deus para com ele ao longo de sua vida.

Joseph Addison, nascido em 1º de maio de 1672, foi um ensaísta inglês, poeta e homem de letras. A respeito de seu nascimento, descobrimos que ele “apareceu fraco e improvável de viver”, diz o Sr. Tyers.* E que “foi posto como morto assim que nasceu.” Sem dúvida, a providência de Deus preservou a sua vida jovem e lhe concedeu quase meio século para servi‑Lo na terra. Era o filho mais velho de Lancelot Addison, um homem muito culto e ministro em sua igreja. Seu pai, sendo um homem estudioso, certificou‑se de que seu filho Joseph tivesse uma boa educação. Ele iniciou seus estudos em sua cidade natal de Milston, em Wiltshire, na Inglaterra.

Enquanto estava na escola por volta de 1685, o jovem de 13 anos que viria a escrever o hino conheceu e tornou‑se grande amigo de Richard Steele, ambos com apenas alguns meses de diferença de idade. Continuaram a amizade ao longo dos anos e, 27 anos depois, de 1711 a 1712, cofunda­ram a revista The Spectator, na qual este hino foi publicado pela primeira vez.

Após passar por várias escolas, Addison foi para Oxford quando tinha cerca de 15 anos. Enquanto esteve lá, continuou a crescer em aprendizado e habilidade, especialmente nas áreas de escrita de poemas e ensaios em latim. Quando tinha 22 anos, em 1694, também começou a mostrar talento na escrita de poesia em inglês.

Um dos detalhes mais notáveis de sua vida que lhe transmitiu a misericórdia de Deus foi como conseguiu escapar por pouco de um terrível naufrágio. Foi essa tragédia e seu assustador relato de sobrevivência que inspiraram a redação deste hino edificante.

Aqui está o hino com os 13 versos originais:

Quando todas as Tuas misericórdias, ó meu Deus,
Minha alma nascente contempla,
Transportado com a visão,
Fico perdido em maravilha, amor e louvor.

Tua Providência sustentou minha vida,
E supriu todas as minhas necessidades,
Enquanto no ventre silencioso jazia,
E pendurado sobre o seio.

A todas as minhas fracas queixas e clamores
Tua misericórdia emprestou um ouvido,
Antes que meus pensamentos débeis tivessem aprendido,
A se formar em oração.

Incontáveis confortos à minha alma
Tua ternura concedeu,
Antes que meu coração infantil concebesse
De Quem aqueles confortos fluíam.

Quando nos caminhos escorregadios da juventude
Com passos descuidados eu corri,
Teu braço invisível transportou‑me em segurança,
E conduziu‑me até a maturidade.

Através de perigos ocultos, trabalhos e mortes,
Ele suavemente desobstruiu meu caminho;
E através das agradáveis armadilhas do vício,
Mais temíveis do que elas.

Ó como as palavras com igual calor
Declararão a gratidão,
Que arde dentro do meu coração extasiado?
Mas tu podes lê‑la ali.

Tua mão generosa com bens mundanos
Fez minha taça transbordar;
E, num Amigo gentil e fiel,
Dobrou todo meu tesouro.

Dez mil, dez mil dádivas preciosas
Minhas graças diárias empregam;
Nem a última é um coração alegre
Que prova essas dádivas com júbilo.

Quando desgastado pela enfermidade, muitas vezes Tu
Renovaste a saúde em meu rosto;
E, quando em pecados e tristezas afundado,
Reviveste minha alma com graça.

Através de cada período da minha vida
Tua bondade seguirei
E depois da morte, em mundos distantes,
O glorioso tema renovarei.

Quando a natureza falhar, e dia e noite
Já não dividirem mais Tuas obras,
Meu sempre agradecido coração,
Ó Senhor, adorará a Tua misericórdia.

Por toda a eternidade a Ti
Um cântico jubiloso elevarei;
Pois, ah, a eternidade é curta demais
Para pronunciar todo o Teu louvor!

Enquanto nos esforçamos para compreender a vida e a história do hino­lógo, vamos fazer um breve exame de algumas decepções que enfrentou. Solteiro até aos 40 e poucos anos, teve esperanças de um dia ter um casamento feliz. Seu casamento com Charlotte, viúva há 15 anos, não correu como ele havia previsto. Diz‑se que o cortejo foi longo e ansioso. Casaram‑se em agosto de 1716, em seu 44º ano. Uma citação afirma que “Diz‑se que a conheceu primeiro ao tornar‑se tutor de seu filho. O casamento, se o relato incontestado pode ser creditado, não acrescentou à sua felicidade; nem os encontrou nem os tornou iguais.”* Além de seu casamento aquém do ideal, a perda de seu bom amigo Richard Steele algum tempo depois afetou‑o profundamente.

Por volta do ano de 1717, sua saúde começou a declinar rapidamente, e em março de 1718 teve de renunciar a algumas de suas funções, necessitando grandemente de repouso e quietude. “A doença sob a qual Addison padecia parece ter sido asma. Tornou‑se mais violenta após sua aposentadoria do cargo e agora veio acompanhada de hidropisia. Seu leito de morte foi plácido e resignado, e confortado por aquelas esperanças religiosas que tantas vezes havia sugerido a outros...” *

Uma última nota que incluirei aqui sobre a vida do autor do hino é o relato de seu falecimento. Havia um jovem chamado Lord Warwick, de carácter rude e dissoluto, a quem Addison muitas vezes havia tentado converter à fé, tudo em vão. Perto do fim de sua vida, fez uma última tentativa de impressionar esse jovem quanto à importância do cristianismo. Mandou chamá‑lo para que estivesse presente ao morrer, dizendo: "Enviei‑te para que possas ver como um cristão pode morrer." Não temos registro de como essa experiência afetou o comportamento de Warwick, mas podemos supor que provavelmente o fez. Joseph Addison morreu em Holland House no dia 17 de junho de 1719, seis semanas após seu 47º aniversário. Está enterrado no Poet's Corner da Abadia de Westminster.

Este hino tem várias melodias: “St Peter”, composta por Alexander Robert Reinagle em 1836, é usada no Church Hymnal e no Christian Hymnary. A melodia "Geneva" foi composta por John Cole em 1805. Nasceu em Tewksbury, Inglaterra, e veio para os Estados Unidos na sua infância. Baltimore, Maryland tornou‑se sua casa americana, e lá recebeu educação. Cedo na vida tornou‑se músico e editor musical. Continuou a compor até sua morte. Esta melodia encontra‑se em Zion's Praises, Hymns of the Church e Harmonia Sacra. A melodia "Contemplation", composta por F.A. Gore Ouseley, é mais amplamente usada por grupos evangélicos e outras igrejas. Outros hinos de Joseph Addison incluem "The Lord my Pasture Shall Prepare" e "The Spacious Firmament." Aqui está uma citação final para nos ajudar a entender quem era Joseph Addison e no que ele acreditava. "Sua religião não tem nela nada de entusiástico ou supersticioso; ele não parece nem credulamente fraco nem deliberadamente cético; sua moralidade não é perigosamente frouxa nem impraticavelmente rígida. Todo o encantamento da fantasia e toda a força de argumento são empregados para recomendar ao leitor seu interesse real, o cuidado de agradar ao Autor do seu ser."

*fonte: Wikipedia e hymnary.org

Just reading the title probably brings negative thoughts to your mind. We as humans don’t typically like to be told “no” because it goes against our nature. Sometimes we bring the “no” upon ourselves because of disobedience, such as when God said “no” to Moses. “I pray thee, let me go over, and see the good land . . . But the Lord . . . would not hear me: and the Lord said unto me, Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter” (Deuteronomy 3:25,26).

In Deuteronomy 1:42, God said “no” to Israel. “And the Lord said unto me, Say unto them, Go not up, neither fight; for I am not among you; lest ye be smitten before your enemies”, but they rebelled at His “no.” “And ye returned and wept before the Lord; but the Lord would not hearken to your voice, nor give ear unto you” (Deuteronomy 1:45).

God said “no” to Paul. “And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me” (2 Corinthians 12:7-9).

Let us focus our attention upon prayerful Paul’s acceptance of God’s “no.”

First, acceptance does not mean that the problem does not exist. Paul accepted God’s “no”, but still had the infirmities.

Second, acceptance does not mean woeful resignation. Paul “besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.” We should be persistent, even when God’s answer is not forthcoming. (cf. Luke 18:1-8).

Third, God’s “no” may be necessary to avoid a greater evil or infirmity. Twice, Paul says the thorn in the flesh was given “lest I should be exalted above measure.” Unlike Paul, however, we may not know the purpose for God’s “no,” but we can be assured of His faithfulness and goodness. With Paul, we too may have to endure one thing, which means accepting God’s refusal in order to achieve a higher purpose or benefit.

Fourth, Paul’s weakness, as a result of God’s “no,” made him strong. “Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). The sorrow and suffering some endure has indeed made them strong in the Lord and in the power of His might.

Fifth, Paul’s infirmity allowed the power of Christ to rest upon him. God’s strength was complete, sufficient, and made perfect in weakness. Paul’s strength was seen to be of God. Therefore, Christ, not Paul, was glorified. The infirmities that Paul endured revealed the power not of himself but of God.

Sixth, God explained his answer of “no” by saying, “My grace is sufficient for thee.” God’s love and acceptance of us, His strength and power to assist us in our infirmities and with our weaknesses, is sufficient and complete.

Seventh, Paul gloried in his infirmities, but only after he accepted God’s “no.” Paul ultimately saw that this allowed God’s power to rest upon him. Paul’s weakness displayed and magnified divine power in a manner that human adequacy and personal sufficiency could never accomplish.

Eighth, unfortunately for him, Paul was the vessel, the sufferer, who had to endure afflictions that God’s grace, power, and glory might be truly reflected, but he was glad to bear it for those purposes (cf. 2 Co 4:7-11; Gal 4:13,14; 6:14,17). Until we are ready to do the same, we cannot accept or understand God’s “no.”

A “no” may come into our life for many various reasons.

When God says, “No,” the Christian must remember:

That God will do right. “He is … a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he” (Deuteronomy 32:4). One may not see; he may not, as Job did not, understand, but God will do right. “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25).

That God’s ways are not ours. “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts” (Isaiah 55:8,9). God sees the end from the beginning. Nothing is hidden from him. “Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it” (Psalms 139:6). as a little child cries in protest when his mother pulls him from the road (It is such a great place to ride a tricycle!), so we may cry when God says, “No,” but He, like the child’s parent, knows danger the child may not be able to comprehend or appreciate fully.

That prayer has a chief purpose. Prayer should not be an attempt to manipulate the will of God. “Not my will, but thine, be done,” the suffering Savior cried, but when God says, “No,” we often forget that fact and complain in effect, “Not Thy will but mine be done.” Perhaps the supreme purpose of prayer is to seek God’s will for our lives, our wants, our needs, and our desires. It will help to remember that when God says “no.”

That a present “no” may be a “yes” in development. Paul was told that he was going to Rome (Acts 19:21; 23:11). But the bars of incarceration, the shackles of servitude, and the jaws of death seemed to say otherwise. Two years of confinement were not convincing evidence of a trip to Rome, nor was a hopeless sea voyage (Acts 24:27; 27:20). However, as we all know, Paul went to Rome (Acts 28:16)!

That God’s laws prevail. The laws of nature are laws of God. God does not will that one to fall off a cliff, but if certain physical laws are broken, he will. God has biological laws. Disease may be contracted, and suffering and death may follow. One may pray, “Give us this day our daily bread,” but if he does not use God’s laws to procure it, or if he contradicts God’s means of acquiring it, he will not receive it. As painful as it is to accept, we frequently are victims of earthly laws in the various and diverse orders of physical life. Of course, the reverse is also true. We often are blessed by the material laws of God (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17; 1 Timothy 5:23).

In conclusion, Job of old bore the lashes of unparalleled human calamity and agony and torture of mind, body, and soul. His faithfulness and steadfast endurance have blessed thirty centuries of sorrowing humanity. Stephen and James met untimely, violent deaths (Acts 7; 12). They died when we would have had them to live. By their suffering and death, the early disciples were shown the power of the new faith, that men could die and yet live in victory. Hence, multiplied millions have been emboldened and have accepted torture and death rather than denounce their faith and hope of eternal life.

Deliverance came. No, not to Stephen and James, nor to suffering servants such as Job, of like precious faith, but it came in unquenchable hope, in the hope that maketh not ashamed. It came through Him that is able to deliver us who, through fear of death, were subject to bondage. “Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.”
