I doubt that there is a soul alive that has not been offended at one time or another. The persistent weeds of evil influence seem to sprout at every corner, testing the best of blooming relationships. The more communication tools we possess, the more miscommunication we seem to encounter, and people are offended. Ministers of the Gospel today are expected to be soft and effeminate lest they offend their listeners. While we certainly must meet people where they are and seek not to offend them, the bane of the modern church is not the bold and offensive minister.

I wish to give no license to hardhearted preachers who are void of tenderness and tears. Woe be unto the dry-eyed prophets who wield the sword of the Lord without an ounce of consideration that there are real people between the ears that they are chopping off in the process. Yet, it seems that there is an epidemic of our day that has surpassed the bubonic plague, outstripped the damage of polio, and makes our modern cancer appear like a minor inconvenience. I speak to the outbreak of the millions of offended hearts that are arising from the rubbish of the innumerable hordes of broken and strained relationships about us on every hand. Jesus mentioned that one of the signs of the end times is that “then shall many be offended . . . and shall hate one another” (Matthew 24:10). Divorce-riddled homes have risen to an all-time high, producing a generation of immense mistrust and pain. Couples will deem themselves as incompatible and separate at the slightest offense. Christians will spend years outside a church setting because they have been offended by fellow believers.

Many will automatically side with the offended party, assuming them to be a victim. Many times they are. “Woe unto the world because of offences!” (Matthew 18:7) But the equation changes when we consider that the sinless Christ offended many. He told His disciples that they must eat His flesh and many left Him. He informed the inner 12 that had stuck with Him, “All ye shall be offended because of me this night” (Mark 14:27). The Pharisees were offended when Christ exposed their vain worship, and Jesus offended His own countrymen simply by doing good. The Greek word is skandalízō meaning “to scandalize”.1 In Hebrew, it means “a stumbling block”. The problem is that many today will stumble over the slightest obstruction in their path and the molehill becomes a mountain.

“Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them” (Psalm 119:165). What shall we say then to this passage? Here are people who have learned how to walk upon the rocky path of life without going down every time a discomfiting obstacle arises before them. We wish to heap no condemnation upon the sensitive soul, but the word sensitive is not in the Bible. The closest word we can find there is sensual, which is very similar in its roots and means natural. Christ described these plants as having “not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Matthew 13:20-21). It is so easy and very natural to feel sorry for the offended. They carry a tremendous sob story, and they usually share it in tears. “In many things, we offend all” (James 3:2). No one is as sinless in their offending as Christ, so there is usually an element of truth poured out against the offender. It seems to me that we all would be much further down the road if we would withhold some of our sympathy for the offended and spend our energies teaching them how to walk upright on the path of life despite the jagged and copious stumbling stones that greet us daily upon our journey. We will learn to live life unoffended when we learn to . . .

Walk Worthy

“I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love” (Ephesians 4:1-2). To walk worthy, as Paul describes it here, is to walk in humility. “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). The more pride-laden our vessel, the more apt we are to be offended. The more honestly we appraise our worth, the less offended we shall be when derided. More humble equals less stumble. When we are accused of a wrong, it always hurts. Jesus says that we should be happy when people say all manner of evil against us falsely. While such a demeaning wound may fester under our skin, there is a condition that is far worse. That is when people say all evil against us truly. Many accusations against us carry a certain percentage of truth in them. It is this portion that the Lord would have us to reckon with, rather than decrying the overstatement. While these falsities levied against us may raise our ire, they are not the reason we stumble and walk around with consequential bruises. Offense arises when the opinion of another doesn't measure up to the extent we tout ourselves.

“Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumbling block out of the way of my people. For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones” (Isaiah 57:14-15). Here, Isaiah instructs us to remove the stumbling block but makes no mention of the offender. The antidote is to be of a contrite and humble spirit. We will never be able to exterminate every avenue of offense. But if reckoned correctly, there is no offense that shall ever be able to divert us from the promise, “they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). It is predominantly our pride which stands in the way of our successful journey, rather than ill-treatment.

Walk In Love

“And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet smelling savour. But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints; neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting . . .” (Ephesians 5:2-4). It takes no scholar to observe the stumblings of a selfish fool. This selfish ambition to obtain friends, wealth, and affluence is guaranteed to bring a man flat on his nose at some time or another. The trail of sins mentioned here are all following in tow to the gratifying of self. King Ahasuerus counseled of Haman on how to honor a worthy man. Haman’s narcissistic mind immediately brooded, “To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?” (Esther 6:6). God had other plans thus the man who was so offended by Mordecai was hung upon the gallows of his own creation. Selfish souls can point to a thousand and one reasons why they are not attaining their aspirations. Somebody wronged them. An unfortunate turn of events derailed them. But it was not Mordecai, Esther, nor even Ahasuerus that brought Haman stumbling to his bitter end. It was his own refusal to walk in love and to sacrifice himself for others that wrought the malignant demise in his soul.

Walk as Children of Light

“Walk as children of light . . . proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Ephesians 5:8-11). Our innate passions contain the third rock of offense. There may be things that we believe are acceptable to our Lord, which are not. There are those who have “itching ears; and they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” (2 Timothy 4:3-4). This may affect those with the most noble intentions and firm beliefs. Christ forewarned His disciples that they would be put out of the synagogues so that when it happened, they “should not be offended” (John 16:1-4).

John the Baptist was a burning and a shining light and no prophet born of women had risen greater. He walked worthy of his calling, baptized the Lord, and rebuked the Pharisees. He walked in love, and multitudes “were willing for a season to rejoice in his light” (John 5:35). Yet the day came when he sent his disciples to ask Jesus: Art thou he that should come? Or look we for another? To which Jesus replied, “Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached ... and blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me” (Luke 7:20-23). Christ's response would indicate that this apparently did not fully fit the aspirations of what John had in mind, and he was struggling to accept it. Like his Old Testament counterpart, Elijah, these like passions provided the fodder for the flames of discouragement. It seemed to John that evil had enveloped the nation and God wasn't doing His part.

We may mean well, but our own passionate feelings are not a good gauge of proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. Phaltiel was a dear soul who fell into such deceit. He had been given Michal by King Saul himself. The princess was no doubt a delicate and pleasing prize. David had evidently valued her so, for he risked his life and doubled the dowry with two hundred Philistine foreskins to secure her hand in marriage. But Phaltiel thought nothing of that, relishing his own good fortune and so enjoyed her company for years. Though this arrangement may have been socially acceptable at the time, no man has the right to receive what another has no right to give. The day came when “they sent, and took her from her husband, even from Phaltiel the son of Laish. And her husband went with her along weeping behind her” (2 Samuel 3:15-16). We know very little of Phaltiel, but if we dismiss ourselves from his emotional avalanche, we must declare him faulty. We dare not let our compassionate heart turn toward him or toward anyone who is offended when asked to separate from works of darkness. When these passionate feelings are allowed to rule, offense is the inevitable result. “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? But if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God” (1 Peter 2:20) . . .

Walk Circumspectly

“See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise” (Ephesians 5:15). “Be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men” (1 Corinthians 14:20). Herein we must honestly acknowledge that ignorance is not bliss. To enter the narrow gate may require a broad mind. Not so broad to allow sin, but broad enough to allow God. Circumspect is a compound word formed from the Latin words circum (around) and spectare (to behold). The one-dimensional soul will spend his days being offended, for he cannot see from the viewpoint of any but his own. There are over a dozen solid scriptures warning us against doing what is right in our own eyes. We must learn to honestly consider the counsel and wisdom of others lest we fall into condemnation.

In her early years, Michal loved David with deep and fervent loyalty but later fell prey to rash judgment. “As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal, Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart” (2 Samuel 6:16). As Michal viewed the scene from her upper vantage, there were two things evident. First, David was exuberantly thankful, and his joy knew no bounds. This is first love, “for whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God” (2 Corinthians 5:13). Second, during David's ecstatic dancing in his loin cloth, his discretion elapsed, and his flesh became a bit public. This would require great circumspection to view from another portal, and Michal will have none of it. Upon his entrance to bless his house, David was met with a blast of pent-up bigotry from his offended and sarcastic wife. While the accusation carried a dimension of truth, to cling to it as supreme was shameful prejudice. God had no sympathy for it and “therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death” (2 Samuel 6:23). Many a good woman has judged her man from her singular corner and parched the soil of the home with the same arid judgment. This narrow-mindedness will never be fruitful no matter how blatant the accusation. There is a correct way to express concern, but the outpouring of biased judgment will turn a celestial oasis into a barren wasteland in a prompt fashion.

“A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle” (Proverbs 18:19). So it is with a sister, husband, wife, friend, etc. While causes for offense abound on every side, does Christ desire us to be offended? Will He salute our sour and shriveled soul? Perhaps He gave us this test so that we may have root within ourselves, “that no man should be moved by these afflictions” (1 Thessalonians 3:3). While we may not be able to control our feelings during times of inward pain, we each can choose a redemptive path and walk in the Spirit. It is a choice to broadcast grievances, nurse hurts, withdraw from the offender, and decline to believe all things. Like the brother offended, these contentions serve to lock the soul like the bars of a castle. But who holds the power for release?

Dubito che esista un’anima viva che non sia stata offesa prima o poi. Le persistenti erbacce dell’influsso del male sembrano spuntare ad ogni angolo, mettendo alla prova le migliori relazioni fiorenti. Più strumenti di comunicazione possediamo, più incomprensioni sembra che incontriamo, e la gente si offende. Oggi dai ministri del Vangelo ci si aspetta che siano docili ed effeminati per non offendere gli ascoltatori. Pur dovendo certamente incontrare le persone dove sono e cercare di non offenderle, il male della chiesa moderna non è il ministro audace e offensivo.

Non intendo dare licenza ai predicatori dal cuore duro privi di tenerezza e di lacrime. Guai ai profeti dagli occhi asciutti che brandiscono la spada del Signore senza un’oncia di considerazione per le persone reali tra le orecchie che stanno recidendo nel processo. Eppure, sembra che vi sia un’epidemia nei nostri giorni che ha superato la peste bubbonica, ha surclassato i danni della poliomielite e fa apparire il nostro cancro moderno come un fastidio minore. Parlo dell’epidemia dei milioni di cuori offesi che sorgono dai rifiuti delle innumerevoli orde di relazioni spezzate e tese che ci circondano in ogni direzione. Gesù menzionò che uno dei segni dei tempi finali è che “allora molti saranno scandalizzati… e odieranno gli uni gli altri” (Matteo 24:10). Le case lacerate dal divorzio sono salite a un livello record, producendo una generazione di immensa sfiducia e dolore. Le coppie si riterranno incompatibili e si separeranno al minimo torto. I cristiani staranno fuori dalla chiesa per anni perché si sono offesi per altri credenti.

Molti si schiereranno automaticamente con la parte offesa, supponendola vittima. Molte volte lo è. “Guai al mondo per gli scandali!” (Matteo 18:7) Ma l’equazione cambia quando consideriamo che il Cristo senza peccato ha offeso molti. Egli disse ai suoi discepoli che dovevano mangiare la sua carne e molti lo lasciarono. Informò i Dodici che erano rimasti con lui: “Voi tutti sarete scandalizzati a causa mia questa notte” (Marco 14:27). I farisei si sentirono offesi quando Cristo espose la loro vana adorazione, e Gesù offese i suoi stessi compatrioti semplicemente facendo del bene. La parola greca è skandalízō, che significa “scandalizzare”.1 In ebraico significa “un inciampo, un ostacolo”. Il problema è che molti oggi inciampano al minimo ostacolo sul loro cammino e la talpa diventa una montagna.

“Grande pace hanno quelli che amano la tua legge: e nulla li scandalizzerà” (Salmo 119:165). Che dobbiamo allora dire di questo passo? Qui ci sono persone che hanno imparato a camminare sul sentiero roccioso della vita senza cadere ogni volta che un ostacolo sgradevole si presenta davanti a loro. Non desideriamo caricare di condanna l’anima sensibile, ma la parola sensibile non è nella Bibbia. La parola più vicina che vi possiamo trovare è sensuale, che ha radici simili e significa naturale (dal latino sensus), intesa più come "sensibile/naturale" nel senso etimologico, non con il significato moderno di "di natura sessuale". Cristo descrisse queste pianticelle come “che non hanno radice in se stessi, ma durano un poco; perché quando viene la tribolazione o la persecuzione a motivo della parola, subito si offendono” (Matteo 13:20-21). È così facile e molto naturale provare compassione per gli offesi. Portano con sé una tremenda storia di dolore, e di solito la condividono in lacrime. “In molte cose tutti erriamo” (Giacomo 3:2). Nessuno è tanto senza peccato nel suo offenderti quanto Cristo, quindi di solito vi è un elemento di verità riversato contro l’offensore. Mi pare che tutti noi saremmo molto più avanti se trattenessimo un po’ della nostra simpatia per gli offesi e spendessimo le nostre energie nell’insegnare loro come camminare dritti sul sentiero della vita nonostante le pietre aguzze e copiose che ci attendono ogni giorno lungo il nostro viaggio. Impareremo a vivere senza offenderci quando impareremo a…

Camminare degnamente

“Io dunque, prigioniero del Signore, vi esorto a camminare in maniera degna della vocazione con cui siete chiamati, con tutta umiltà e mansuetudine, con pazienza, sopportandovi gli uni gli altri con amore” (Efesini 4:1-2). Camminare degnamente, come Paolo lo descrive qui, è camminare nell’umiltà. “L’orgoglio precede la rovina, e lo spirito altezzoso precede la caduta” (Proverbi 16:18). Più il nostro vaso è carico d’orgoglio, più siamo inclini a offenderci. Più onestamente valutiamo il nostro valore, meno ci offenderemo quando veniamo derisi. Più siamo umili, meno inciampiamo. Quando veniamo accusati di un torto, fa sempre male. Gesù dice che dobbiamo essere felici quando la gente dice ogni sorta di male contro di noi falsamente. Benché una tale ferita umiliante possa suppurare sotto la nostra pelle, esiste una condizione molto peggiore. È quando la gente dice tutto il male contro di noi veramente. Molte accuse contro di noi contengono una certa percentuale di verità. È questa parte che il Signore vorrebbe che noi esaminassimo, piuttosto che deprecare l’esagerazione. Pur se tali falsità mosse contro di noi possono suscitare il nostro sdegno, esse non sono la ragione per cui inciampiamo e andiamo in giro con lividi consequenziali. L’offesa nasce quando l’opinione di un altro non è all’altezza di quella che noi esaltiamo di noi stessi.

“Raddrizzate, raddrizzate la via, togliete di mezzo gli impedimenti dalla via del mio popolo. Perché così parla l’Altissimo e l’Eccelso che abita l’eternità, il cui nome è Santo: io abito nell’altissimo e nel santo luogo, e con il contrito e umile di spirito, per ravvivare lo spirito degli umili e per ravvivare il cuore dei contriti” (Isaia 57:14-15). Qui Isaia ci istruisce a rimuovere l’ostacolo ma non fa menzione dell’offensore. L’antidoto è avere uno spirito contrito e umile. Non riusciremo mai a sterminare ogni via di offesa. Ma se calcoliamo correttamente, non vi sarà offesa che possa mai sviare dalla promessa: “ma quelli che sperano nel Signore acquistano nuove forze; sollevano ali come aquile; corrono e non si stancano; camminano e non si affaticano” (Isaia 40:31). È prevalentemente il nostro orgoglio a stare sulla via del nostro viaggio vittorioso, più che il cattivo trattamento.

Camminare nell’amore

“E camminate nell’amore, come anche Cristo ci ha amati e ha dato se stesso per noi in offerta e sacrificio a Dio, in odore soave. Ma l’impudicizia e ogni impurità o cupidigia non si nomini nemmeno tra di voi, come si conviene ai santi; né oscenità, né sciocche conversazioni, né schernimenti…” (Efesini 5:2-4). Non serve un dottore per osservare gli inciampi di un sciocco egoista. Questa ambizione egoistica di ottenere amici, ricchezze e agiatezza è garantita per far capitombolare l’uomo prima o poi. La scia di peccati qui menzionati segue tutti il conseguimento del soddisfacimento di sé. Il re Assuero consigliò ad Aman su come onorare un uomo degno. La mente narcisistica di Aman subito pensò tra sé: “A chi piacerebbe il re onorare più che a me?” (Ester 6:6). Dio aveva altri progetti e così l’uomo che si era tanto offeso per Mardocheo fu impiccato sulla forca della sua stessa creazione. Le anime egoiste possono indicare mille e una ragione per cui non raggiungono le loro aspirazioni. Qualcuno li ha offesi. Un sfortunato colpo di eventi li ha sviati. Ma non fu Mardocheo, né Ester, né nemmeno Assuero a far cadere Aman nel suo tragico fine. Fu il suo rifiuto di camminare nell’amore e di sacrificarsi per gli altri che provocò la rovina maligna nella sua anima.

Camminare come figli della luce

“Camminate come figli della luce… esaminando ciò che è gradito al Signore. E non partecipate alle opere infruttuose delle tenebre, ma piuttosto riprovatele” (Efesini 5:8-11). Le nostre passioni innate contengono la terza roccia dell’offesa. Ci possono essere cose che crediamo siano accettabili al nostro Signore, e che non lo sono. Ci sono quelli che hanno “orecchie che prudono; e si volgeranno dalle verità alle favole” (2 Timoteo 4:3-4). Questo può colpire anche coloro che hanno le intenzioni più nobili e convinzioni salde. Cristo avvertì i suoi discepoli che sarebbero stati cacciati dalle sinagoghe così che quando ciò fosse accaduto, “non si scandalizzassero” (Giovanni 16:1-4).

Giovanni il Battista era una lampada che ardeva e splendeva e nessun profeta nato da donna è stato più grande. Camminò degno della sua vocazione, battezzò il Signore e rimproverò i farisei. Camminò nell’amore, e moltitudini “furono disposte per un tempo a rallegrarsi nella sua luce” (Giovanni 5:35). Eppure giunse il giorno in cui mandò i suoi discepoli a chiedere a Gesù: “Sei tu colui che deve venire? O dobbiamo aspettare un altro?” Al che Gesù rispose: “Andate e riferite a Giovanni quello che voi udite e vedete: i ciechi ricuperano la vista, i monchi camminano, i lebbrosi sono mondati, i sordi odono, i morti risorgono, ai poveri è annunciato il vangelo… e beato chiunque non si scandalizza di me” (Luca 7:20-23). La risposta di Cristo indicherebbe che questo apparentemente non corrispondeva pienamente alle aspirazioni che Giovanni aveva in mente, e che egli stava lottando per accettarlo. Come il suo corrispondente dell’Antico Testamento, Elia, queste passioni fornirono il combustibile per le fiamme dello scoraggiamento. A Giovanni pareva che il male avesse invaso la nazione e che Dio non stesse facendo la sua parte.

Possiamo avere buone intenzioni, ma i nostri stessi sentimenti appassionati non sono una buona misura per esaminare ciò che è gradito al Signore. Faltiele era un’anima cara che cadde in tale inganno. Gli era stata data Mical dallo stesso re Saul. La principessa era senza dubbio un premio delicato e piacevole. Davide evidentemente l’aveva così apprezzata che rischiò la vita e raddoppiò la dote con duecento foreskin filistei per ottenere la sua mano in matrimonio. Ma Faltiele non tenne conto di ciò, godendo della sua buona sorte e apprezzandone la compagnia per anni. Anche se questa disposizione poteva essere socialmente accettabile all’epoca, nessun uomo ha il diritto di ricevere ciò che un altro non ha il diritto di dare. Giunse il giorno in cui “mandarono, e la presero dal marito, da Faltiele figlio di Laish. E il marito la seguì con pianto dopo di lei” (2 Samuele 3:15-16). Sappiamo molto poco di Faltiele, ma se ci asteniamo dall’immergerci nella sua valanga emotiva, dobbiamo dichiararlo in errore. Non dobbiamo lasciare che il nostro cuore compassionevole si volga verso di lui o verso chiunque si offenda quando gli si chiede di separarsi dalle opere delle tenebre. Quando questi sentimenti appassionati sono lasciati a regnare, l’offesa è il risultato inevitabile. “Perché quale gloria è, se quando fate il male e siete castigati, lo sopportate? Ma se quando fate il bene e soffrite per questo, lo sopportate, questo è gradito a Dio” (1 Pietro 2:20)…

Camminare con circospezione

“Guardate dunque con attenzione come vi comportate, non da stolti ma da saggi” (Efesini 5:15). “Non siate bambini nell’intelletto; siate però negli istinti bambini, ma nel senno uomini” (1 Corinzi 14:20). Qui dobbiamo riconoscere onestamente che l’ignoranza non è beatitudine. Entrare per la porta stretta può richiedere una mente ampia. Non tanto ampia da permettere il peccato, ma abbastanza ampia da permettere Dio. Circospezione è una parola composta formata dal latino circum (intorno) e spectare (guardare). L’anima unidimensionale passerà i suoi giorni offesa, perché non può vedere dal punto di vista di nessuno se non del proprio. Ci sono più di una dozzina di solide Scritture che ci avvertono di non fare ciò che è giusto ai nostri occhi. Dobbiamo imparare onestamente a considerare il consiglio e la saggezza degli altri, non senza il rischio di cadere in condanna.

Nei suoi primi anni, Mical amava Davide con profonda e fervente lealtà ma cadde poi vittima di giudizi avventati. “Quando l’arca dell’Eterno entrò nella città di Davide, Mical, figlia di Saul, guardò dalla finestra e vide il re Davide saltare e danzare davanti all’Eterno; e lo disprezzò nel suo cuore” (2 Samuele 6:16). Mentre Mical osservava la scena dalla sua altezza, furono evidenti due cose. Primo, Davide era esuberantemente riconoscente e la sua gioia non aveva limiti. Questa è la prima carità, “poiché se siamo fuori di noi, è per Dio” (2 Corinzi 5:13). Secondo, durante la danza estatica di Davide in perizoma, la sua discrezione venne meno e la sua carne divenne un poco pubblica. Questo avrebbe richiesto grande circospezione per essere visto da un altro portale, e Mical non ne volle sapere. Al suo ingresso per benedire la sua casa, Davide fu accolto da un’esplosione di bigotteria repressa dalla sua moglie offesa e sarcastica. Mentre l’accusa portava una dimensione di verità, aggrapparvisi come suprema fu un vergognoso pregiudizio. Dio non ebbe simpatia per questo e “perciò Mical figlia di Saul non ebbe figlio fino al giorno della sua morte” (2 Samuele 6:23). Molte buone donne hanno giudicato il loro uomo dal loro angolo singolare e hanno prosciugato il suolo della casa con lo stesso giudizio arido. Questa mentalità ristretta non sarà mai feconda per quanto palese sia l’accusa. C’è un modo giusto di esprimere preoccupazione, ma lo sfogo di un giudizio fazioso trasformerà un’oasi celeste in un deserto in breve tempo.

“Un fratello offeso è più difficile da riconquistare che una città forte: e le loro contese sono come i paletti di una fortezza” (Proverbi 18:19). Così è per una sorella, marito, moglie, amico, ecc. Sebbene le cause di offesa abbondino da ogni parte, Cristo desidera forse che siamo offesi? Saluterà la nostra anima acida e rinsecchita? Forse ci diede questa prova affinché possiamo avere radice dentro di noi, “che alcuno non sia smosso da queste afflizioni” (1 Tessalonicesi 3:3). Pur se non possiamo controllare i nostri sentimenti durante i tempi di dolore interiore, ciascuno di noi può scegliere una via redentrice e camminare nello Spirito. È una scelta divulgare i torti, coltivare i dolori, ritirarsi dall’offensore e rifiutare di credere ogni cosa. Come il fratello offeso, queste contese servono a chiudere l’anima come le sbarre di una fortezza. Ma chi detiene il potere per la liberazione?

I doubt that there is a soul alive that has not been offended at one time or another. The persistent weeds of evil influence seem to sprout at every corner, testing the best of blooming relationships. The more communication tools we possess, the more miscommunication we seem to encounter, and people are offended. Ministers of the Gospel today are expected to be soft and effeminate lest they offend their listeners. While we certainly must meet people where they are and seek not to offend them, the bane of the modern church is not the bold and offensive minister.

I wish to give no license to hardhearted preachers who are void of tenderness and tears. Woe be unto the dry-eyed prophets who wield the sword of the Lord without an ounce of consideration that there are real people between the ears that they are chopping off in the process. Yet, it seems that there is an epidemic of our day that has surpassed the bubonic plague, outstripped the damage of polio, and makes our modern cancer appear like a minor inconvenience. I speak to the outbreak of the millions of offended hearts that are arising from the rubbish of the innumerable hordes of broken and strained relationships about us on every hand. Jesus mentioned that one of the signs of the end times is that “then shall many be offended . . . and shall hate one another” (Matthew 24:10). Divorce-riddled homes have risen to an all-time high, producing a generation of immense mistrust and pain. Couples will deem themselves as incompatible and separate at the slightest offense. Christians will spend years outside a church setting because they have been offended by fellow believers.

Many will automatically side with the offended party, assuming them to be a victim. Many times they are. “Woe unto the world because of offences!” (Matthew 18:7) But the equation changes when we consider that the sinless Christ offended many. He told His disciples that they must eat His flesh and many left Him. He informed the inner 12 that had stuck with Him, “All ye shall be offended because of me this night” (Mark 14:27). The Pharisees were offended when Christ exposed their vain worship, and Jesus offended His own countrymen simply by doing good. The Greek word is skandalízō meaning “to scandalize”.1 In Hebrew, it means “a stumbling block”. The problem is that many today will stumble over the slightest obstruction in their path and the molehill becomes a mountain.

“Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them” (Psalm 119:165). What shall we say then to this passage? Here are people who have learned how to walk upon the rocky path of life without going down every time a discomfiting obstacle arises before them. We wish to heap no condemnation upon the sensitive soul, but the word sensitive is not in the Bible. The closest word we can find there is sensual, which is very similar in its roots and means natural. Christ described these plants as having “not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Matthew 13:20-21). It is so easy and very natural to feel sorry for the offended. They carry a tremendous sob story, and they usually share it in tears. “In many things, we offend all” (James 3:2). No one is as sinless in their offending as Christ, so there is usually an element of truth poured out against the offender. It seems to me that we all would be much further down the road if we would withhold some of our sympathy for the offended and spend our energies teaching them how to walk upright on the path of life despite the jagged and copious stumbling stones that greet us daily upon our journey. We will learn to live life unoffended when we learn to . . .

Walk Worthy

“I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love” (Ephesians 4:1-2). To walk worthy, as Paul describes it here, is to walk in humility. “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). The more pride-laden our vessel, the more apt we are to be offended. The more honestly we appraise our worth, the less offended we shall be when derided. More humble equals less stumble. When we are accused of a wrong, it always hurts. Jesus says that we should be happy when people say all manner of evil against us falsely. While such a demeaning wound may fester under our skin, there is a condition that is far worse. That is when people say all evil against us truly. Many accusations against us carry a certain percentage of truth in them. It is this portion that the Lord would have us to reckon with, rather than decrying the overstatement. While these falsities levied against us may raise our ire, they are not the reason we stumble and walk around with consequential bruises. Offense arises when the opinion of another doesn't measure up to the extent we tout ourselves.

“Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumbling block out of the way of my people. For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones” (Isaiah 57:14-15). Here, Isaiah instructs us to remove the stumbling block but makes no mention of the offender. The antidote is to be of a contrite and humble spirit. We will never be able to exterminate every avenue of offense. But if reckoned correctly, there is no offense that shall ever be able to divert us from the promise, “they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). It is predominantly our pride which stands in the way of our successful journey, rather than ill-treatment.

Walk In Love

“And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet smelling savour. But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints; neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting . . .” (Ephesians 5:2-4). It takes no scholar to observe the stumblings of a selfish fool. This selfish ambition to obtain friends, wealth, and affluence is guaranteed to bring a man flat on his nose at some time or another. The trail of sins mentioned here are all following in tow to the gratifying of self. King Ahasuerus counseled of Haman on how to honor a worthy man. Haman’s narcissistic mind immediately brooded, “To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?” (Esther 6:6). God had other plans thus the man who was so offended by Mordecai was hung upon the gallows of his own creation. Selfish souls can point to a thousand and one reasons why they are not attaining their aspirations. Somebody wronged them. An unfortunate turn of events derailed them. But it was not Mordecai, Esther, nor even Ahasuerus that brought Haman stumbling to his bitter end. It was his own refusal to walk in love and to sacrifice himself for others that wrought the malignant demise in his soul.

Walk as Children of Light

“Walk as children of light . . . proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Ephesians 5:8-11). Our innate passions contain the third rock of offense. There may be things that we believe are acceptable to our Lord, which are not. There are those who have “itching ears; and they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” (2 Timothy 4:3-4). This may affect those with the most noble intentions and firm beliefs. Christ forewarned His disciples that they would be put out of the synagogues so that when it happened, they “should not be offended” (John 16:1-4).

John the Baptist was a burning and a shining light and no prophet born of women had risen greater. He walked worthy of his calling, baptized the Lord, and rebuked the Pharisees. He walked in love, and multitudes “were willing for a season to rejoice in his light” (John 5:35). Yet the day came when he sent his disciples to ask Jesus: Art thou he that should come? Or look we for another? To which Jesus replied, “Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached ... and blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me” (Luke 7:20-23). Christ's response would indicate that this apparently did not fully fit the aspirations of what John had in mind, and he was struggling to accept it. Like his Old Testament counterpart, Elijah, these like passions provided the fodder for the flames of discouragement. It seemed to John that evil had enveloped the nation and God wasn't doing His part.

We may mean well, but our own passionate feelings are not a good gauge of proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. Phaltiel was a dear soul who fell into such deceit. He had been given Michal by King Saul himself. The princess was no doubt a delicate and pleasing prize. David had evidently valued her so, for he risked his life and doubled the dowry with two hundred Philistine foreskins to secure her hand in marriage. But Phaltiel thought nothing of that, relishing his own good fortune and so enjoyed her company for years. Though this arrangement may have been socially acceptable at the time, no man has the right to receive what another has no right to give. The day came when “they sent, and took her from her husband, even from Phaltiel the son of Laish. And her husband went with her along weeping behind her” (2 Samuel 3:15-16). We know very little of Phaltiel, but if we dismiss ourselves from his emotional avalanche, we must declare him faulty. We dare not let our compassionate heart turn toward him or toward anyone who is offended when asked to separate from works of darkness. When these passionate feelings are allowed to rule, offense is the inevitable result. “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? But if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God” (1 Peter 2:20) . . .

Walk Circumspectly

“See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise” (Ephesians 5:15). “Be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men” (1 Corinthians 14:20). Herein we must honestly acknowledge that ignorance is not bliss. To enter the narrow gate may require a broad mind. Not so broad to allow sin, but broad enough to allow God. Circumspect is a compound word formed from the Latin words circum (around) and spectare (to behold). The one-dimensional soul will spend his days being offended, for he cannot see from the viewpoint of any but his own. There are over a dozen solid scriptures warning us against doing what is right in our own eyes. We must learn to honestly consider the counsel and wisdom of others lest we fall into condemnation.

In her early years, Michal loved David with deep and fervent loyalty but later fell prey to rash judgment. “As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal, Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart” (2 Samuel 6:16). As Michal viewed the scene from her upper vantage, there were two things evident. First, David was exuberantly thankful, and his joy knew no bounds. This is first love, “for whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God” (2 Corinthians 5:13). Second, during David's ecstatic dancing in his loin cloth, his discretion elapsed, and his flesh became a bit public. This would require great circumspection to view from another portal, and Michal will have none of it. Upon his entrance to bless his house, David was met with a blast of pent-up bigotry from his offended and sarcastic wife. While the accusation carried a dimension of truth, to cling to it as supreme was shameful prejudice. God had no sympathy for it and “therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death” (2 Samuel 6:23). Many a good woman has judged her man from her singular corner and parched the soil of the home with the same arid judgment. This narrow-mindedness will never be fruitful no matter how blatant the accusation. There is a correct way to express concern, but the outpouring of biased judgment will turn a celestial oasis into a barren wasteland in a prompt fashion.

“A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle” (Proverbs 18:19). So it is with a sister, husband, wife, friend, etc. While causes for offense abound on every side, does Christ desire us to be offended? Will He salute our sour and shriveled soul? Perhaps He gave us this test so that we may have root within ourselves, “that no man should be moved by these afflictions” (1 Thessalonians 3:3). While we may not be able to control our feelings during times of inward pain, we each can choose a redemptive path and walk in the Spirit. It is a choice to broadcast grievances, nurse hurts, withdraw from the offender, and decline to believe all things. Like the brother offended, these contentions serve to lock the soul like the bars of a castle. But who holds the power for release?

Ik betwijfel of er een ziel leeft die niet eens of andermaal gekrenkt is geweest. De hardnekkige onkruiden van kwade invloed lijken op elke hoek te ontspruiten en beproeven de beste bloeiende relaties. Hoe meer communicatiemiddelen we bezitten, hoe meer miscommunicatie we schijnbaar tegenkomen, en mensen voelen zich gekwetst. Tegenwoordige predikanten van het Evangelie worden verondersteld zacht en effeminé te zijn, opdat zij hun luisteraars niet zouden kwetsen. Terwijl we zeker mensen moeten tegemoetkomen waar ze zijn en proberen hen niet te kwetsen, is het verderf van de moderne kerk niet de gedurfde en aanstootgevende prediker.

Ik wil geen vrijbrief geven aan hardhartige predikanten die geen tederheid en tranen kennen. Wee die droge-ogige profeten die het zwaard des Heren hanteren zonder ook maar een greintje consideratie dat er echte mensen tussen de oren zitten die zij in het proces afgehakt hebben. Toch lijkt er een epidemie van onze tijd te zijn die de builenpest heeft overtroffen, de schade van polio heeft ingehaald en onze moderne kanker als een klein ongemak doet voorkomen. Ik spreek over de uitbraak van de miljoenen gekrenkte harten die oprijzen uit het puin van de ontelbare hordes verbroken en gespannen relaties om ons heen aan alle kanten. Jezus noemde dat een van de tekenen van de eindtijd is dat “dan zullen velen aanstoot nemen . . . en zij zullen elkaar haten” (Mattheüs 24:10). Huizen geteisterd door echtscheiding zijn tot een recordhoogte gestegen en hebben een generatie van immense wantrouwen en pijn voortgebracht. Echtparen zullen zichzelf onverenigbaar verklaren en zich al bij het kleinste misbaar scheiden. Christenen zullen jaren buiten een kerksamenkomst doorbrengen omdat zij gekrenkt zijn door medegelovigen.

Velen zullen automatisch partij kiezen met de gekwetste partij en hen als slachtoffer beschouwen. Vaak zijn zij dat ook. “Wee de wereld vanwege de aanstoot!” (Mattheüs 18:7) Maar de vergelijking verandert als we overwegen dat de zondeloze Christus velen heeft gekwetst. Hij zei zijn discipelen dat zij Zijn vlees moesten eten en velen verlieten Hem. Hij vertelde de binnenste twaalf die bij Hem waren gebleven: “Gij allen zult dezen nacht aanstoot aan mij nemen” (Marcus 14:27). De Farizeeën raakten verontwaardigd toen Christus hun ijdele aanbidding ontblootte, en Jezus beledigde Zijn landgenoten eenvoudig door goed te doen. Het Griekse woord is skandalízō, wat “schandaliseren” betekent.1 In het Hebreeuws betekent het “een struikelblok”. Het probleem is dat velen vandaag over het geringste obstakel struikelen en het molshoopje een berg wordt.

“Grote vrede hebben zij die uw wet liefhebben: en niets zal hen aanstoot geven” (Psalm 119:165). Wat moeten we dan zeggen van deze passage? Hier zijn mensen die hebben geleerd hoe ze op het rotsachtige pad des levens kunnen wandelen zonder elke keer neer te gaan wanneer een ongemakkelijk struikelblok zich voor hen voordoet. We willen geen veroordeling ophopen over de gevoelige ziel, maar het woord gevoelig staat niet in de Bijbel. Het dichtstbijzijnde woord dat we daar kunnen vinden is zinnelijk, dat in zijn wortels zeer gelijkaardig is en natuurlijk betekent. Christus beschreef deze gewassen als die “geen wortel in zichzelf hebben, maar duren voor een tijd: want wanneer verdrukking of vervolging opkomt om des woords wil, terstond neemt hij aanstoot” (Mattheüs 13:20-21). Het is zo gemakkelijk en heel natuurlijk om medelijden te voelen met de gekrenkte. Zij dragen een enorm klaagverhaal, en ze delen het gewoonlijk in tranen. “In vele dingen struikelen wij allen” (Jakobus 3:2). Niemand is zo zondeloos in het krenken als Christus, dus is er gewoonlijk een element van waarheid naar de overtreder uitgestort. Het lijkt mij dat we veel verder op de weg zouden zijn als we wat van ons medeleven voor de gekwetste zouden terughouden en onze energie zouden besteden aan hen te leren hoe oprecht te wandelen op het levenspad ondanks de scherpe en talrijke struikelstenen die ons dagelijks op onze reis begroeten. We zullen leren onberoerd te leven wanneer we leren . . .

Waardig Wandelen

“Ik dan, de gevangene des Heren, smeek u, dat gij wandelt waardig naar de roeping waarmee gij geroepen zijt, met alle ootmoedigheid en zachtmoedigheid, met lijdzaamheid, verdragend elkander in liefde” (Efeziërs 4:1-2). Waardig wandelen, zoals Paulus het hier beschrijft, is wandelen in nederigheid. “Trots gaat voor de val, en een hoogmoedige geest voor een struikeling” (Spreuken 16:18). Hoe meer trots het vaartuig belast, des te vatbaarder zijn wij om gekwetst te worden. Hoe eerlijker wij onze waarde inschatten, des te minder zullen we gekwetst zijn wanneer we bespot worden. Meer nederig betekent minder struikel. Wanneer wij van een kwaad beschuldigd worden, doet het altijd pijn. Jezus zegt dat we blij moeten zijn wanneer mensen allerlei kwaad tegen ons spreken onder valse beschuldiging. Hoewel zo’n vernederende wond onder onze huid kan etteren, is er een toestand die veel erger is. Dat is wanneer mensen werkelijk al het kwade over ons zeggen. Veel beschuldigingen tegen ons dragen een bepaald percentage waarheid in zich. Het is dit gedeelte waarmee de Heer wil dat wij rekening houden, in plaats van de overdrijving aan te klagen. Terwijl deze onwaarheden jegens ons onze woede kunnen opwekken, zijn zij niet de reden dat wij struikelen en rondlopen met nare blauwe plekken. Aanstoot ontstaat wanneer de mening van een ander niet opweegt tegen de mate waarin wij onszelf ophemelen.

“Bouw op, bouw op, bereid de weg, neem het struikelblok weg uit de weg van mijn volk. Want aldus zegt de hoge en verhevene, Die de eeuwigheid bewoont, wiens naam heilig is: Ik woon in den hoge en in den heilige plaats; en bij hem, die een verslagen en een nederig van geest is, om den geest der nederigen te leven geven, en het hart der verslagenen te verkwikken” (Jesaja 57:14-15). Hier instrueert Jesaja ons het struikelblok weg te nemen maar noemt geen woord over de overtreder. Het tegengif is een verslagen en nederig geest te zijn. We zullen nooit elk pad van aanstoot kunnen uitroeien. Maar indien juist gerekend, zal er geen aanstoot zijn die ons ooit van de belofte kan afbrengen: “zij zullen vliegen met vleugels als arenden; zij zullen lopen en niet moe worden; zij zullen wandelen, en niet mat worden” (Jesaja 40:31). Het is voornamelijk onze trots die in de weg staat van onze succesvolle reis, eerder dan slechte behandeling.

Wandel in Liefde

“En wandelt in de liefde, gelijk ook Christus ons liefgehad heeft, en Zichzelven voor ons heeft overgegeven, tot een offerande en een slachtoffer tot een welriekende reuk voor God. Maar hoererij, en alle onreinheid, of geldzucht, laat het niet eens genoemd worden onder u, gelijk het heiligen betaamt; ook geen vuile praat, noch dwaas spreken, noch zotternij . . .” (Efeziërs 5:2-4). Je hebt geen geleerde nodig om de struikelingen van een egoïstische dwaas te zien. Deze egoïstische ambitie om vrienden, rijkdom en welstand te verkrijgen, brengt een mens gegarandeerd op enig moment plat op zijn neus. Het spoor van zonden dat hier genoemd wordt volgt allen in de kielzog van het bevredigen van het zelf. Koning Ahasveros raadpleegde Haman hoe hij een begaafd man zou eren. Hamans narcistische geest broedde onmiddellijk: “Aan wie zou de koning meer behagen om eer te doen dan aan mijzelf?” (Esther 6:6). God had andere plannen, en zo werd de man die zich zo gekwetst voelde door Mordechai opgehangen aan de galg van zijn eigen schepping. Egoïstische zielen kunnen duizend en één redenen aanwijzen waarom zij hun aspiraties niet bereiken. Iemand heeft hen onrecht gedaan. Een ongelukkige wending der gebeurtenissen heeft hen ontspoord. Maar het waren niet Mordechai, Esther, noch zelfs Ahasveros die Haman tot zijn bittere einde hebben gebracht. Het was zijn eigen weigerachtigheid om in liefde te wandelen en zich voor anderen op te offeren die de kwaadaardige ondergang in zijn ziel teweegbracht.

Wandel als Kinderen des Lichts

“Wandelt als kinderen des lichts . . . beproevende wat des Heren is welgevallig. En hebt geen gemeenschap met de onvruchtbare werken der duisternis, maar vermaant ze veeleer” (Efeziërs 5:8-11). Onze aangeboren hartstochten bevatten de derde steen van aanstoot. Er kunnen dingen zijn die wij geloven dat de Here toelaat, die Hij niet toelaat. Er zijn zij die “jeukende oren zullen hebben; en zij zullen de waarheid van zich afwenden, en zich tot fabelen wenden” (2 Timoteüs 4:3-4). Dit kan diegenen treffen met de meest nobele bedoelingen en vaste overtuigingen. Christus voorwaarschuwde Zijn discipelen dat zij uit de synagogen gezet zouden worden zodat, wanneer het gebeurde, zij “niet zouden aanstoot nemen” (Johannes 16:1-4).

Johannes de Doper was een brandend en schijnend licht en geen profeet die uit vrouwen geboren was, is groter opgestaan. Hij wandelde waardig naar zijn roeping, doopte de Heer, en bestrafte de Farizeeën. Hij wandelde in liefde, en menigten “waren voor een tijd bereid zich te verblijden in zijn licht” (Johannes 5:35). Toch kwam de dag dat hij zijn discipelen zond om Jezus te vragen: Zijt Gij Degene die komen zou? Of zullen wij een andere verwachten? Waarop Jezus antwoordde: “Gaat heen en berichtt Johannes hetgeen gij gehoord en gezien hebt; de blinden zien, de manke wandelen, de melaatsen worden rein, de doven horen, de doden worden opgewekt, aan de armen wordt het evangelie gepredikt ... en zalig is die niet aanstoot neemt in Mij” (Lucas 7:20-23). Christus’ antwoord zou erop wijzen dat dit blijkbaar niet geheel voldeed aan de verwachtingen die Johannes voor ogen had en dat hij moeite had dit te aanvaarden. Zoals zijn Oudtestamentische tegenhanger, Elia, gaven zulke hartstochten brandstof aan de vlammen van ontmoediging. Het leek Johannes dat het kwaad de natie had omhuld en dat God Zijn deel niet deed.

We menen het misschien goed, maar onze eigen hartstochtelijke gevoelens zijn geen goede graadmeter om te beproeven wat des Heren welgevallig is. Paltiel was een dierbare ziel die in zulk bedrog viel. Hij was Michal gegeven door koning Saul zelf. De prinses was ongetwijfeld een tere en aangename prijs. David had haar kennelijk zo gewaardeerd, want hij riskeerde zijn leven en verdubbelde de bruidsschat met tweehonderd Filistijnse voorhuiden om haar hand in huwelijk te verkrijgen. Maar Paltiel gaf daar niets om, genoot van zijn eigen geluk en genoot jarenlang van haar gezelschap. Hoewel deze regeling sociaal acceptabel geweest kan zijn in die tijd, heeft geen mens het recht te ontvangen wat een ander geen recht heeft te geven. De dag kwam dat “zij zonden, en namen haar van haar man, ja van Paltiel, den zoon van Laïs. En haar man ging met haar mee, en weende achter haar aan” (2 Samuel 3:15-16). We weten zeer weinig van Paltiel, maar als we ons van zijn emotionele lawine distantiëren, moeten we hem ondeugdelijk noemen. We mogen ons medelijdend hart niet keren naar hem of naar iemand die gekwetst is wanneer hen gevraagd wordt zich te scheiden van de werken der duisternis. Wanneer deze hartstochtelijke gevoelens de overhand krijgen, is aanstoot het onvermijdelijke resultaat. “Want welke roem is het, indien, wanneer gij zondaars, gij geduldig lijden? Maar zo gij goeds doet en lijdt, en dat geduldig verdraagt, dat is welgevallig voor God” (1 Petrus 2:20) . . .

Wandel Voorzichtig

“Ziet dan nauwgezet, hoe gij wandelt, niet als dwazen, maar als wijzen” (Efeziërs 5:15). “Weest niet kinderen in het verstand: maar in de boosheid zijt gij kinderen, doch in het verstand zijt mannen” (1 Korinthiërs 14:20). Hierin moeten wij eerlijk erkennen dat onwetendheid geen zaligheid is. De smalle poort binnengaan kan een ruim denkvermogen vereisen. Niet zo ruim om zonde toe te staan, maar ruim genoeg om God plaats te geven. Voorzichtig is een samengesteld woord gevormd uit de Latijnse woorden circum (rondom) en spectare (bezien). De eendimensionale ziel zal zijn dagen doorbrengen met zich gekwetst voelen, want hij kan niet zien vanuit enig ander gezichtspunt dan het zijne. Er zijn meer dan een dozijn stevige Schriftplaatsen die ons waarschuwen niet te doen wat goed is in onze eigen ogen. We moeten leren eerlijk het advies en de wijsheid van anderen te overwegen, opdat wij niet in veroordeling vallen.

In haar vroege jaren hield Michal David lief met diepe en vurige trouw maar viel later ten prooi aan overhaaste oordeelvorming. “Terwijl de ark des Heren in de stad David kwam, keek Michal, de dochter van Saul, door een venster en zag koning David springen en dansen voor de HEERE; en zij verachtte hem in haar hart” (2 Samuel 6:16). Terwijl Michal de scène van haar hogere uitkijkpost bekeek, waren er twee dingen evident. Ten eerste was David uitbundig dankbaar en kende zijn vreugde geen grenzen. Dit is eerste liefde, “want of wij onszelven onnozel maken, het is ter ere Gods” (2 Korinthiërs 5:13). Ten tweede, tijdens Davids extatische dans in zijn lendendoek, verviel zijn discretie en werd zijn vlees enigszins openbaar. Dit zou grote voorzichtigheid vergen om vanuit een ander venster te bezien, en Michal wilde daar niets van weten. Bij zijn intrede om zijn huis te zegenen, werd David geconfronteerd met een uitbarsting van opgebouwde vooroordeel van zijn gekrenkte en sarcastische vrouw. Hoewel de beschuldiging een dimensie van waarheid droeg, was eraan vasthouden als het opperste schandelijke vooringenomenheid. God had daar geen medelijden mee en “daarom had Michal, de dochter van Saul, geen kind tot op de dag van haar dood” (2 Samuel 6:23). Menige goede vrouw heeft haar man veroordeeld vanuit haar enge hoek en de bodem van het huis doodgebrand met dezelfde dorstige beoordeling. Deze bekrompenheid zal nooit vruchtbaar zijn, hoe flagrant de beschuldiging ook is. Er is een juiste manier om bezorgdheid te uiten, maar het uitstorten van bevooroordeeld oordeel zal een hemelse oase in een dor woestijn veranderen op korte termijn.

“Een gekwetste broer is moeilijker te winnen dan een sterke stad: en hun twist zijn als de ijzeren staven van een vesting” (Spreuken 18:19). Zo is het met een zuster, echtgenoot, vrouw, vriend, enzovoort. Hoewel oorzaken voor aanstoot aan alle kanten overvloedig zijn, verlangt Christus dat wij gekwetst zijn? Zal Hij onze zure en verschrompelde ziel groeten? Misschien gaf Hij ons deze beproeving opdat wij wortel in onszelf zouden hebben, “opdat niemand bewogen worde door deze verdrukkingen” (1 Thessalonicenzen 3:3). Hoewel wij onze gevoelens tijdens innerlijke pijn niet onder controle kunnen hebben, kan ieder van ons een verlossende weg kiezen en in de Geest wandelen. Het is een keuze om klachten uit te zenden, wonden te verzorgen, zich terug te trekken van de overtreder, en te weigeren alle dingen te geloven. Zoals de gekwetste broer sluiten deze twistingen de ziel op als de staven van een vesting. Maar wie houdt de macht tot bevrijding?

When I was converted, I had never heard the term Anabaptist. I had never heard much about witnessing to others. I remember thinking about all my friends who didn’t know anything about what had just happened to me. My girlfriend of seven years didn’t understand. One thing kept going through my mind: “I need to tell them!” Something good had happened to me, and everyone needed to know that the same could happen to them! I remember a time when my brother and I were thinking of a place where we could tell many people about Jesus. We decided to go to a major league baseball game. I was nervous, I was scared, and I will never forget what happened. I had never spoken in front of a large crowd before, but when I opened my mouth, God filled it.

I did not only go and talk to people I did not know. When I saw an old friend, I would tell them what happened to me. They would usually say they had heard it before and try to convince me to settle down and relax. I will be the first to admit that I made some mistakes in those first few years. I noticed, to my astonishment, that while many people didn’t like me, it was the people who said they were Christians who appeared to dislike me the most. One day I was visiting with an older man who said he had been a Christian most of his life. During the discussion, he pointed up to a lightbulb and said, “‘Do you see that lightbulb? It’s not speaking.” I was shocked. He was telling me that, yes, while Jesus says we are the light of the world, lights are supposed to shine quietly. They don’t speak.

I was astonished. Was this true? I went home to do a Bible study. It wasn’t long before I found verses like Matthew 4:23, “And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.” Then in Matthew 9, when Jesus “saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd. Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few; Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:36-38).

It seems to me that wherever Jesus went, He was talking to people about the kingdom. I have seen people witnessing about God, but sometimes in an offensive way. But does that mean we shouldn’t witness? If you read the book of Acts, that’s nearly all you see—the Gospel going out! In one account the authorities captured the disciples and said they could go free if they would only be quiet. However, the disciples said they could not. “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20). Later they were silenced—by death.

Sometime later I heard about these people called Anabaptists. As I studied them, I began to see how they too, would not be silent. I ordered a copy of The Martyr’s Mirror and was astounded when I read about these people who lived like the disciples. They fulfilled the things Jesus said, “And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). And in Romans 8:36, “As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.”

Dear brothers and sisters, I believe the fire is going out. I hear many of our Anabaptist people talking about living a quiet and peaceable life. Jesus tells us in the parable of the sower, “He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful” (Matt. 13:22). Could that be where many of us are at? We live in the free land of America where money seems easy to obtain. Is it possible we have become deceived by our own wealth and the cares of this world? Have we become like the world to avoid being persecuted by it?

Many years ago, a group of Anabaptists fled persecution and moved to a country where there was less oppression. They opened a furniture shop to support themselves, but they couldn’t sell any furniture because they were the dreaded Anabaptists. Soon, the situation became desperate because they didn’t have money to buy food. One day a wealthy man walked into the shop. All the workers stopped what they were doing. They thought to themselves, “Maybe this man will buy something, and we can eat!” An old brother approached the possible client and asked him if he knew Jesus. After a short chat, the man stormed out of the store in a fit of anger. The hungry workers asked the old man why he had scared away their only chance at a sale. He explained that for this man to know Jesus was far more important than for them to earn some money.

In the mindset of the early Anabaptists, the Gospel of Jesus was number one. As in Acts, they could not but speak of the things they had seen and heard. And they, too, were “killed all the day long”.

So, what do we do with the verse about a quiet and peaceable life? The verse is found in 1 Timothy 2:1-2: “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.” What did the apostle Paul mean when he wrote this? Did he mean that we should be quiet about the gospel and never challenge a sinner? It is hard to believe that Paul is telling us to do something he never did, something that Christ Himself never did. In fact, no one in the scriptures who followed God was quiet about their faith. In numerous accounts of early Christians who had been arrested for their faith, the authorities would plead with them to just be quiet! But they refused, just as the disciples did. They also chose death, rather than a quiet and peaceable life.

One young Anabaptist who was arrested left behind his dear wife expecting their first child. The authorities waited for the child to be born then brought the infant to the new father in prison. They told him he was now a father and could go home and be with his wife and son. He could even continue to believe the same way, but he had to keep quiet and not speak out against sin in the state church. The young father refused. For him, being quiet was not an option. They burned him at the stake.

So, what does 1 Timothy 2:1-2 mean? It seems that the Christians in the Bible and early church were all about spreading the gospel, all about the church of Christ. They went about preaching the gospel, holding meetings in the mountains, woods, or anywhere people would come. That was their life. In the verse in 1 Timothy 2, Paul is saying we should pray that the authorities will let us live in peace so we can spread the gospel. Christians should be out spreading the word and pressing into the kingdom. Our prayer is that the authorities will let us live in peace, while we serve the Prince of peace.

Today it’s easy to be a Christian when you settle down and live a quiet and peaceable life, never challenging a sinner or correcting a brother. But who said it would be easy?

When we were living in Haiti, we taught our church about the cost of following Jesus. It was amazing to hear the Haitians’ testimonies of applying Jesus’ teaching to their lives. One time, two members told us they were about to lose their jobs because of following the gospel. To hear them make a stand for following truth made me happy. Another sister in the church told me that the school her children attended wore uniforms and the girls were required to wear pants. When she sent her daughter to school in a modest dress, she came home with a note from the principal saying she was not to return to school wearing that thing.

1 Peter 4:14 says, “If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.”

True joy comes from suffering. Suffering comes from obeying Jesus. Are we too busy with trivial matters while the world goes to hell? Let us follow Jesus like the early Christians, where men could not deny that the power of God was working in them. We have something everyone needs. What are we waiting for? Let’s reunite, gather back together, deny ourselves, take up the cross, and follow Him!

जब मेरा जीर्णोद्धार हुआ, तब मैंने कभी शब्द "अनाबाप्टिस्ट" नहीं सुना था। मैंने दूसरों को साक्षी देने के बारे में भी ज्यादा कुछ नहीं सुना था। मुझे याद है कि मैं उन सभी मित्रों के बारे में सोचता था जो मेरे साथ जो हुआ था उसके बारे में कुछ भी नहीं जानते थे। मेरी सात साल की प्रेमिका समझ नहीं पा रही थी। एक बात मेरे मन में बार-बार घूमती रहती थी: “मुझे उन्हें बताना चाहिए!” मेरे साथ कुछ अच्छा हुआ था, और सबको जानना चाहिए था कि वही उनके साथ भी हो सकता है! मुझे वह समय याद है जब मेरा और मेरे भाई का विचार था कि हम किसी ऐसे स्थान पर जाएँ जहाँ हम कई लोगों से यीशु के बारे में बात कर सकें। हमने एक मेजर लीग बेसबॉल के खेल पर जाने का निर्णय लिया। मैं घबरा रहा था, मैं डर रहा था, और मैं कभी उस घटना को नहीं भूल सकता। मैंने कभी भी एक बड़े जनसमूह के सामने नहीं बोला था, पर जब मैंने मुंह खोला, तो परमेश्वर ने उसे भर दिया।

मैं केवल अनजान लोगों से ही बात करने नहीं गया। जब मैं किसी पुराने मित्र से मिलता, तो मैं उन्हें बताता कि मेरे साथ क्या हुआ। वे आमतौर पर कहते कि वे यह पहले सुन चुके हैं और मुझे शांत होकर बस बैठ जाने के लिए मनाते। मैं सबसे पहले स्वीकार करूँगा कि उन पहले कुछ वर्षों में मैंने कुछ गलतियाँ कीं। मुझे आश्चर्य हुआ कि जबकि कई लोग मुझे पसंद नहीं करते थे, पर वे लोग जो खुद को ईसाई कहते थे, वे मुझे सबसे अधिक नापसंद करते दिखे। एक दिन मैं एक बड़े उम्र वाले व्यक्ति से मिल रहा था जिसने कहा कि वह अपने अधिकांश जीवन काल से ईसाई रहा है। बातचीत के दौरान उसने ऊपर एक बल्ब की ओर इशारा किया और कहा, "क्या तुम उस बल्ब को देखते हो? वह बोल नहीं रहा।" मैं स्तब्ध रह गया। वह मुझे यह बता रहा था कि, हाँ, जबकि यीशु कहते हैं कि हम संसार की रोशनी हैं, बत्तियाँ चुपचाप चमकती हैं। वे बोलती नहीं हैं।

मैं चकित था। क्या यह सच था? मैं घर जाकर बाइबल का अध्ययन करने बैठा। बात देर न लगी कि मुझे मत्ती 4:23 जैसे छंद मिल गए, “और यीशु सारे गलील में जा कर उनके सभाघरों में सिखाता और राज्य के सुसमाचार का उपदेश करता और लोगों के बीच सब प्रकार की रोग-बीमारियों को चंगा करता रहा।” फिर मत्ती 9 में, जब यीशु “भीड़ को देखकर दया खाई, क्योंकि वे थके हुए और चारों ओर बिखरे हुए थे, जैसे कि बिना चरवाहे के भेड़ें। तब उसने अपने शिष्यों से कहा, ‘‘कृषि तो वास्तव में बहुत है, पर मजदूर थोड़े हैं; अतः तुम्ही फसल के स्वामी से प्रार्थना करो कि वह अपने फसल में मजदूर भेजे’’ (मत्ती 9:36-38)।

मेरे लिए ऐसा प्रतीत होता है कि जहाँ भी यीशु गए, वे लोगों से राज्य के बारे में बोल रहे थे। मैंने लोगों को परमेश्वर के बारे में साक्षी देते देखा है, पर कभी-कभी आक्रामक ढंग से। पर क्या इसका अर्थ यह है कि हमें साक्षी नहीं देना चाहिए? यदि आप प्रेरितों के काम की पुस्तक पढ़ें, तो आप लगभग वही देखते हैं—सुसमाचार बाहर जा रहा है! एक किस्से में अधिकारियों ने शिष्यों को पकड़कर कहा कि वे मुक्त हो सकते हैं यदि वे केवल चुप रहेंगे। पर शिष्यों ने कहा कि वे नहीं कर सकते। "क्योंकि हम वे बातें जो हमने देखीं और सुनीं, कहने से रोक नहीं सकते" (प्रेरितों के काम 4:20)। बाद में उन्हें चुप कराया गया—मृत्यु द्वारा।

कुछ समय बाद मैंने इन लोगों के बारे में सुना जिन्हें अनाबाप्टिस्ट कहा जाता था। जब मैंने उनका अध्ययन किया, तो मैंने देखा कि वे भी चुप न रहने वाले थे। मैंने The Martyr’s Mirror का एक प्रति मँगवाई और जब मैंने उन लोगों के बारे में पढ़ा जो शिष्यों की तरह रहते थे तो मैं दंग रह गया। उन्होंने यीशु द्वारा कही गई बातों को पूरा किया, “और तुम्हें सब मनुष्यों द्वारा मेरे नाम के कारण घृणित किया जाएगा; पर जो अंत तक दृढ़ रहता है वही उद्धार पाएगा” (मत्ती 10:22). और रोमियों 8:36 में, “जैसा कि लिखा है, तेरे कारण हम दिन भर मारे जाते हैं; हम कोष्टी के लिए भेड़ों के समान गिठाणी माने जाते हैं।”

प्रिय भाइयों और बहनों, मुझे लगता है कि हमारी आराधना की आग बुझती जा रही है। मैं सुनता हूँ कि हमारे कई अनाबाप्टिस्ट लोग शांत और शांतिपूर्ण जीवन जीने की बात कर रहे हैं। यीशु हमें सीड बोने वाले की मिसाल में कहते हैं, “जो लोग कांटों के बीच बीज पाते हैं वे ऐसे हैं जो वचन सुनते हैं; पर इस संसार की चिंता और धन की छलना वचन को घुटन करते हैं और वह अनुत्पादक हो जाता है” (मत्ती 13:22)। क्या कईों की स्थिति यही हो सकती है? हम अमेरिका की आज़ाद भूमि में रहते हैं जहाँ धन प्राप्त करना आसान प्रतीत होता है। क्या संभव है कि हम अपनी ही समृद्धि और इस जगत की चिंताओं से धोखा खा गए हों? क्या हमने उत्पीड़न से बचने के लिए स्वयं को संसार जैसा बना लिया है?

कई वर्ष पहले, एक समूह अनाबाप्टिस्टों ने उत्पीड़न से भागकर एक देश में शरण ली जहाँ दमन कम था। उन्होंने अपनी आजीविका के लिए एक फर्नीचर की दुकान खोली, पर वे कोई फर्नीचर बेच नहीं पाए क्योंकि वे डरे हुए अनाबाप्टिस्ट थे। जल्द ही स्थिति संकटपूर्ण हो गई क्योंकि उनके पास खाने के लिए पैसे नहीं थे। एक दिन एक संपन्न व्यक्ति दुकान में प्रवेश किया। सभी काम करने वाले लोग जो कर रहे थे वह रोक दिए। उन्होंने सोचा, “शायद यह आदमी कुछ खरीद लेगा, और हम खा सकेंगे!” एक बूढ़ा भाई संभावित ग्राहक के पास गया और उससे पूछा क्या वह यीशु को जानता है। थोड़ी बातचीत के बाद वह आदमी गुस्से में दुकान से बाहर भाग गया। भूखे कामगारों ने बूढ़े आदमी से पूछा कि तुमने हमारे केवल संभावित बिक्री के मौके को क्यों भगा दिया। उसने समझाया कि इस आदमी का यीशु को जानना उनके लिए कुछ पैसे कमाने से कहीं अधिक महत्वपूर्ण था।

प्रारंभिक अनाबाप्टिस्टों की मानसिकता में, यीशु का सुसमाचार पहले स्थान पर था। प्रेरितों के काम की तरह, वे उन बातों के बारे में बोलने से रोक नहीं सकते थे जो उन्होंने देखी और सुनी थीं। और वे भी “दिन भर मारे जाते थे।”

तो, हम 1 तिमोथियुस 2:1-2 के बारे में क्या करते हैं जहाँ शांत और शांतिपूर्ण जीवन का उल्लेख है? यह छंद इस प्रकार है: “मैं अतः प्रस्ताव करता हूँ कि पहले से सब प्रकार की विनती, प्रार्थना, मध्यस्थता, और धन्यवाद की भेंटें लोगों के लिए की जाएँ; यहाँ तक कि राज्याओं के लिए और सभी अधिकारियों के लिए; ताकि हम सारे भक्ति और ईमानदारी में शांत और शांतिपूर्ण जीवन व्यतीत कर सकें।” पौलुस ने जब यह लिखा तब उसका क्या अर्थ था? क्या उसका अभिप्राय यह था कि हमें सुसमाचार के बारे में चुप रहना चाहिए और कभी पापी को चुनौती नहीं देनी चाहिए? यह मानना कठिन है कि पौलुस हमसे ऐसा करने को कह रहे हों जो उसने स्वयं कभी नहीं किया, ऐसा कुछ जो मसीह स्वयं ने कभी नहीं किया। वस्तुतः पवित्रग्रंथों में परमेश्वर का अनुसरण करने वाले किसी भी व्यक्ति के बारे में ऐसा नहीं दिखता कि वे अपने विश्वास के बारे में चुप रहे हों। प्रारंभिक ईसाइयों के कई लेखों में जब उन्हें उनके विश्वास के लिए गिरफ्तार किया गया, तो अधिकारी उनसे केवल चुप रहने के लिए कहकर विनती करते थे! पर वे इनकार कर देते थे, जैसे शिष्यों ने किया था। उन्होंने भी शांत और शांतिपूर्ण जीवन के बजाय मृत्यु को चुना।

एक युवा अनाबाप्टिस्ट जिसे गिरफ्तार किया गया था, उसने अपनी प्रिय पत्नी को एक बच्चे की उम्मीद करते हुए पीछे छोड़ दिया। अधिकारियों ने बच्चे के जन्म का इंतज़ार किया और फिर शिशु को जेल में नए पिता के पास लाया। उन्होंने उसे कहा कि अब वह पिता है और घर जाकर अपनी पत्नी और पुत्र के साथ रह सकता है। वह वही विश्वास करना भी जारी रख सकता था, पर उसे चुप रहना होगा और राज्य की चर्च में पाप के विरुद्ध बोलना बंद करना होगा। उस युवा पिता ने मना कर दिया। उसके लिए चुप रहना विकल्प नहीं था। उन्हें उसे चिता पर जला दिया।

तो, 1 तिमोथियुस 2:1-2 का अर्थ क्या है? ऐसा प्रतीत होता है कि बाइबल और प्रारंभिक चर्च के ईसाई सुसमाचार फैलाने के बारे में पूरी तरह समर्पित थे, मसीह की चर्च के बारे में पूरी तरह ध्यान केंद्रित थे। वे सुसमाचार का उपदेश करते रहे, पहाड़ों, जंगलों या जहाँ भी लोग आते वहां सभाएँ रखते रहे। वही उनका जीवन था। 1 तिमोथियुस 2 में पौलुस कह रहा है कि हमें यह प्रार्थना करनी चाहिए कि अधिकारी हमें शांति से जीने दें ताकि हम सुसमाचार फैला सकें। ईसाइयों को बाहर जाकर वचन फैलाना चाहिए और राज्य में भी प्रवेश करना चाहिए। हमारी प्रार्थना यह है कि अधिकारी हमें शांति से जीने दें, जबकि हम शांति के राजकुमार की सेवा कर रहे हैं।

आज सहज हो गया है ईसाई होना जब आप बस शांत और शांतिपूर्ण जीवन बीता कर बैठे रहें, कभी किसी पापी को चुनौती न दें या किसी भाई को सुधार न दें। पर किसने कहा था कि यह आसान होगा?

जब हम हैती में रह रहे थे, हमने अपनी सभा को यीशु का अनुसरण करने की कीमत के बारे में सिखाया। हैतीवासियों के लिए यह देखकर अद्भुत लगा कि वे अपने जीवनों में यीशु की शिक्षाओं को लागू करने की गवाही दे रहे थे। एक बार, दो सदस्यों ने बताया कि वे सुसमाचार का पालन करने के कारण अपनी नौकरियाँ खोने वाले थे। उन्हें सत्य के पालन के लिए खड़ा देखना मेरे लिए सुखद था। एक और बहन ने बताया कि जिस स्कूल में उसके बच्चों को भेजा जाता था वहाँ वर्दी होती और लड़कियों को पैंट पहननी अनिवार्य थी। जब उसने अपनी बेटी को एक विनम्र पोशाक पहनाकर स्कूल भेजा, तो वह प्रधानाचार्य से एक नोट लेकर घर आई जिसमें कहा गया था कि वह उस वस्त्र में लौटकर स्कूल न आए।

1 पतरुस 4:14 कहता है, “यदि तुम्हें मसीह के नाम के कारण तिरस्कार मिला तो तुम धन्य हो; क्योंकि परमेश्वर के महिमा और आत्मा तुम पर विश्राम करती है; जहाँ तक वे लोग हैं, उन पर बुरा कहा जाता है, पर तुम्हारे भाग में तुम महिमित हो।”

सच्ची खुशी दुःख से आती है। दुःख यीशु की आज्ञा मानने से आता है। क्या हम असंगत मामलों में इतने व्यस्त हैं जबकि संसार नर्क की ओर जा रहा है? आइए हम प्रारंभिक ईसाइयों की तरह यीशु का अनुकरण करें, जहाँ लोग नकार न सकें कि परमेश्वर की शक्ति उनके भीतर काम कर रही थी। हमारे पास ऐसा कुछ है जिसकी सबको आवश्यकता है। हम किसका इंतज़ार कर रहे हैं? आइए पुनर्मिलन करें, फिर से एकत्र हों, अपने आप को अस्वीकार करें, क्रूस उठा कर उसके पीछे चलें!
